"Pressure is still falling," she said. "Look at the monitor, not the wound."

Tomas pulled his mask down. He was exhausted, proud, and twenty-six hours into a shift he had volunteered for. "The suture line is dry. We close."

Priya kept her hands on the instrument tray. "His lactate is climbing. I've paged the perfusionist. If you close now and he crashes on the table, I'll be the one who tells his daughter."

"It's going to fall," Daniel whispered. "We're going to fall."

Marco knelt beside him in the aisle. "Hey. Look at me. You're safe. This is what the plane is supposed to do."

"Breathe with me. In for four." Marco counted slowly. "Hold it. Out for six."

Up in the cockpit, Helen watched the altitude tape and the weather radar. She keyed the intercom. "Marco, how's your passenger?"

"Scared, but holding," he replied. "Can we get a smoother altitude?"

"Working on it. Climbing to 37,000 to get above the worst of it." She eased the throttle forward. "Tell him the bumps are normal. We've flown through worse this month."

Marco relayed the message in a calm voice. Daniel nodded at each word, his breath slowly easing.

Ten minutes later the ride smoothed out. The seatbelt sign clicked off. Daniel let go of the armrest and laughed, shaky and embarrassed. "Sorry."

"Don't be," Marco said, returning to his cups. "Most people feel that way the first time. You did great."

Helen, landing her plane in Denver an hour later, said the same thing to her first officer, Sunil Joshi, who had been silent the whole way down.

Harriet nodded slowly. "Then let's be careful with it."

Owen handed her a glass of water. "That was fair," he said.

"It was as fair as I could make it," she replied. "Now go and tell the Moreaus they can go home."

"Exactly. Two sentences and a checkbox."

"And I keep the keys?"

"You keep the keys," she said. "I bring the seven steps down to three."

Kofi laughed, the first sound in an hour. "Fine. But if this breaks in production, you're on the call with me."

Mara was the brave one, always first to the stream, always last to get out of the cold water. Her younger brother, Jonah, was the careful one, the boy who read the trail signs twice and packed spare socks.

They had been walking the Ridgeback trail for three hours when Mara decided to take a shortcut through the fallen pines. "It's faster," she said, already climbing over a log.

"The map is wrong. Come on, Jo."

Mara tried to laugh. "We'll just walk until we find the road."

Jonah sat down on a rock and pulled his jacket tighter. "We don't know where the road is. We could be walking further in."

For the first time, Mara's bravery flickered. She knelt beside him and looked at his shaking hands. "Hey. You always have a plan. What's the plan?"

He took a deep breath, unfolded the map, and traced the stream with his finger. "If we follow the water downhill, it'll lead to the valley road. Water always goes somewhere."

Mara nodded. "Okay. You lead, I'll watch the back."

So they walked in silence, Jonah calling out the bends in the stream, Mara scanning the shadows for danger. Two hours later, headlights flickered through the trees. A park ranger named Denise Ortiz waved them down, shaking her head.

"You two are lucky," she said. "Most people panic and go the wrong way."

Jonah looked at Mara. She grinned, a little shaken. "Guess we're both brave now," she said.

"Better," Marco said, and he meant it. "You?"

"I know, love." Lydia turned back to Frank. "Six five, then."

Frank had expected a fight, and he felt oddly deflated. He had offered her a thousand and a half less than he could have afforded, and she had folded without a single argument.

"You don't have to take that," he said, unable to stop himself. "I'd go to seven."

Lydia shook her head. "Six five is fine. I just want to be home before the storm."

They completed the paperwork in the office. Oliver watched Frank count out the notes with a frown.

"You didn't even make her sweat, Mr. Mercer," he said.

Frank laughed and handed him a receipt. "No. I'm learning that some people just want to go home."

Ms. Helen Marsh had taught for nine days before she admitted she could not match most of the names to the faces. Six students sat together in the third row of Room 14, and she had decided to hold each one in memory by a single detail until the rest came.

Dev Patel wore red trainers that squeaked on the linoleum whenever he shifted in his seat. Priya Raman had a blue ink smudge on her middle finger, and she rubbed it when she was thinking. Tomas Berg whistled softly through his teeth before he spoke, so Helen always knew an answer was coming. Amara Osei wore glasses held together at one hinge with white tape. Lucas Chen coughed into the crook of his elbow every few minutes, apologising with his eyes. Mei Lin filled the margins of every handout with galloping horses, long-maned and improbably leggy.

On Friday Helen asked the row to read a paragraph aloud, one sentence each, and she listened for the detail to match the voice. Red trainers, then Dev's steady reading. A whistle, then Tomas, careful and slow. Amara pushed her taped glasses up and read with precision. Priya read quickly and sure, her finger wiping at the ink.

Lucas read his sentence between coughs, and Helen realised she had been counting the coughs instead of hearing the words. She made a note to listen harder next time.

Mei did not read at all. When Helen reached her desk she was drawing a horse on the back of the page, and the horse was grinning. Helen asked her name, though she already knew it, and Mei looked up and said, "Mei," very quietly, as if testing whether the teacher was going to remember.

Helen smiled and wrote it down beside the galloping horse. By the end of the month she would know all six of them by their voices, but on that Friday their single details were all she had, and she held onto them like handrails.

Arthur set down his knife. He was seventy-nine, a retired builder who had driven the same blue estate for thirty years, and the thought of handing over the keys made his throat tighten.

"I drove to the bakery on Tuesday," he said. "Nobody has to drive me there."

"We know," said Carol gently. "But you took the long way round for an hour and came back without bread. Eileen was worried."

Ben pushed the bread basket towards his father. "We're not taking the car, Dad. We're asking you to think about a bus pass, or a taxi account, or me driving you on Saturdays."

Arthur looked at his son for a long moment. Then he turned to his wife, who had been driving with him to church for fifty years and was now the one who looked frightened.

"Saturdays," he said finally. "But I'm choosing the bread."

Everyone laughed, and the decision was made, and nobody mentioned the gatepost again until Christmas.

Premise: A person who uses a wheelchair decides to climb a mountain with friends.
text:
Jess Holloway had spent six years saying no to mountains. She used a wheelchair, and the hills around her village in Wales had always looked like something other people did. Then her old university friend Matt rang on a grey Tuesday and said, "We're climbing Pen y Fan in May. Come with us."

"In a wheelchair?" Jess said.

"In a chair with some very stubborn friends," Matt replied. "Dee's already bought the rope."

Dee, a physiotherapist, came to visit the following week with a folder of routes and an off-road chair she had borrowed from a charity in Cardiff. She set it beside Jess's kitchen table and grinned. "Thirty-kilo frame, fat tyres, and a brake that actually works."

Over the next month they trained on the local towpath. Matt pushed Jess uphill on the gravel, and his breathing got harder with every bend. Dee taught them to read the ground, to shift weight at the right moment, and to trust the chair.

On the morning of the climb it rained hard. The three of them stood at the car park with their rucksacks, and Jess felt the old fear crawl up her spine. Matt put a hand on her shoulder.

"We go slowly," he said. "We stop when you say stop."

The first hour was brutal. The path turned to scree and then to stone steps, and twice Jess had to be lifted over a gap by Matt and a stranger from a walking group who had stopped to help. But near the top the cloud broke, and the whole valley opened below them, silver with rain and sudden sun.

Jess pushed the wheels forward one more time and laughed out loud. "Okay," she said. "I'll admit it. Mountains are better than I expected."

"What's your name, mate?" Richard asked. "I've been sitting next to you all week and I never asked."

"Eddie," he said. "And you're Richard, from the blue car with the parking ticket."

Richard grinned. "Guilty."

Kayla laughed, wiped her eyes, and went back to her essay.

Silas Greer had kept the Blackrock light for thirty-one years, and in all that time he had never seen the sea like this. The storm came in from the west on a Tuesday night, a black wall of wind that hit the tower before the first gust had even reached the village.

"The glass is holding," he said. "I'll keep it lit."

Hours passed. A wave struck the lower wall so hard that the whole tower shuddered, and dust fell from the ceiling like snow. Silas gripped the rail and counted the seconds until the beam came round again.

Near dawn a fishing boat appeared on the rocks below, its lights blinking wildly. Silas flashed the lamp, slow and steady, the signal he had memorised as a boy, and watched the boat turn toward the safe channel. He never knew who was aboard.

When the sun finally rose over the grey water, the storm was gone. Silas sat down on the iron floor, his back against the cold lens, and laughed quietly at the ceiling. Then he poured the last of the tea, which had gone lukewarm, and drank it anyway.

Sam nodded slowly. "I teach four-year-olds. Nothing gets a number. Yesterday a boy named Otis told me he was a dog until lunchtime, and I had to decide whether that counted as a reason not to sit at the table."

"That's mine," Ruth said. "Finished it in March."

Sam looked at it for a moment, then back at her. "You should come and tell the class. They'd lose their minds."

"Would Otis be a dog?"

"Almost certainly," Sam said, and went to get her a slice of cake.

Premise: A pilot and a flight attendant deal with a passenger who panics during turbulence.

The seatbelt sign chimed just as the first jolt dropped the aircraft like a stone through a lift shaft. In row 23, Walter Briggs grabbed both armrests and began to shout.

"We're going down! Somebody tell me we're not going down!"

Jorge Silva, the senior flight attendant, was strapped into his jump seat by the rear galley. He picked up the interphone. "Captain, I've got a passenger in real distress in 23C. Can you give me anything?"

On the flight deck, Captain Lena Marsh glanced at the weather radar, then at her first officer, Ama Boateng. "Ride reports say it smooths out at thirty-four thousand. Ask for the climb." She keyed the interphone back. "Jorge, eight minutes, maybe less. I'll make an announcement."

Her voice came over the cabin speakers, slow and even. "Folks, this is Captain Marsh. What you're feeling is ordinary mountain wave turbulence. It's uncomfortable, and it's completely safe. We're climbing out of it now."

Walter was not listening. He was trying to unbuckle.

Jorge waited for a lull, then crossed the aisle in three quick steps, crouched beside him, and put a hand flat on the man's seatbelt buckle. "Walter? I'm Jorge. Keep that on for me. Look at my cup."

He set a plastic cup of water on the tray table. It shivered, sloshed, and stayed upright.

"Planes are built to bend," Jorge said. "That's the wings doing their job. Breathe with me. In for four."

Walter breathed. The cup steadied. Somewhere above them, Lena eased the throttles back, and the air went smooth as glass.

"All but these." He pointed at three dishes on the end, where the bacteria had grown in thick, healthy rings. "Which makes no sense. Same strain, same agar, same temperature."

Felix stared at her. Then he climbed onto a stool, a stocky man in socks, and held his phone up to the fixture. An app showed a sharp spike in the ultraviolet range.

"The new bulbs are leaking UV," he whispered. "It's been sterilising my plates."

"So it's not your fault," Rosa said.

"It's a paper," Felix said. "Somebody's going to want to know about this in every lab in the building." He climbed down and grabbed a notebook. "Rosa, how do you spell Delgado? You're going in the acknowledgements."

Margaret Doyle had been clerk to Judge Samuel Achebe for nine years, and she knew he was not ready when he asked for a second cup of tea.

"Both mothers have," Margaret said. "Mrs. Reid and Mrs. Pearce. They sit four feet apart. They've never spoken."

"I know." He turned the cup in his hands. "Whatever I do today, one of them leaves this building feeling the law has failed her."

Margaret had typed hundreds of his judgments. She had watched him rewrite a single sentence eleven times so that a widow would understand it. She picked up the wig and held it out.

"Then say it plainly," she said. "That's what you're good at. They'll both remember you didn't hide behind the words."

Samuel took the wig, settled it on, and stood. In the corridor he paused at the courtroom door.

"Margaret. Afterwards, will you make sure someone sits with Mrs. Pearce? Not an usher. A person."

"I'll do it myself," she said, and opened the door.

Premise: A programmer and a designer argue about an app the night before launch.
text:
At 11:48 p.m., eleven hours before the Pebble app went live, Owen Price slammed his laptop shut hard enough to wake the office cat.

"You moved my button," he said.

Yuki Tanaka did not look up from her terminal. "I moved your button forty pixels because your button was covering the error message."

"The button was the whole design! Big, round, thumb-height. The entire onboarding flows toward it."

"The onboarding flows toward a crash on Android eight." She swivelled her chair around. "If your network drops while you sign up, the message appears exactly under the button. Nobody can see it. They tap the button again. It sends the request twice. Two accounts, same email, database chokes."

Owen opened his mouth and closed it.

"I'm not saying the button's ugly," Yuki added. "It's a very good button."

"It is a very good button," Owen said sourly. He reopened the laptop. "Can't you fix the double request in the code?"

"I can. I did. Two hours ago. But the user still doesn't know what happened, and that's your department, not mine."

He was quiet for a minute, dragging shapes around in his design file. Then he turned the screen toward her. The error message was no longer a grey line of text; it was a soft yellow banner sliding down from the top, and the button stayed exactly where he had put it.

Yuki studied it. "That's better than mine."

"Everything is better than yours. You use default fonts."

"Ship it," she said, and opened a new branch called owen-was-right-ish.

Finn, who was seven, handed her a screwdriver.

"It's a pinch," Ivy said.

The first pancake stuck. The second one burned. The smoke alarm went off, and Finn ran in from the garage to watch, trailing an oily rag, and wiped his hands on the tea towel Martin was using to fan the alarm.

Jo appeared in the doorway with grease on her cheek and the lawnmower's spark plug held up like a trophy. "Found it. Completely black. What's burning?"

"Breakfast," said Martin.

"Breakfast is purple," said Finn, peering at the pan.

Jo took the spatula, flipped the third pancake perfectly, and handed it back. Martin handed her the nine-millimetre spanner, which he had found in the cutlery drawer.

They ate the purple pancakes in the garden, and the lawnmower did not get fixed until Sunday.

Gareth was crying a little, quietly, but he was writing. When he finished, he handed Mei the note with shaking fingers.

"It wasn't your fault," she said, reading it. "The patch came from the vendor. You did what the checklist said."

The deer was not there. Neither, twenty minutes later, was the path.

"It's fine," Juno said, scrambling up a mossy bank. "The car park's downhill. Everything's downhill from here."

Juno leapt a stream, slipped, and laughed when her trainer filled with water. Ezra did not laugh. He sat down on a log and his eyes stung, and he hated that they stung.

Juno came back and sat next to him, dripping. She didn't say anything for once.

After a minute, Ezra unfolded the map. "The stream," he said, sniffing. "Streams go to the river. The river goes past the car park. It's on here."

"So we follow the water."

"We follow the water. Slowly. And you stay where I can see you."

"Fine," Juno said. "But I'm going first."

"You can go first," Ezra said, "if you hold my hand."

She did, the whole way down, and she only pulled him into the stream once.

Marco went to work as though nothing had happened. He stayed late, then later. He told his colleague Dev that he was "honestly fine, mate, it was mutual," and Dev, who had seen him reply to the same email three times, said nothing.

On the third day, Hannah signed up for a pottery class she had been talking about for a year. Her first bowl collapsed. She kept it anyway.

On the fifth day, Marco went running at six in the morning and found himself outside the Linden Café. He stood across the street and watched the waitress set out chairs at the corner table. He did not go in.

On the seventh day, he collected the box. Hannah wasn't home; her neighbour, Mrs. Osei, handed it over. Inside, on top of the lamp, was his umbrella.

The car was a 2014 Honda Civic with a scrape along one door and a fresh wax job that fooled nobody, least of all Gloria Stamp.

"Thirty-two," she said.

Neil laughed nervously. "It's done ninety thousand miles. That's nothing for a Honda."

"It's done ninety thousand miles on its original clutch," Gloria said. "I can smell it. The tyres need replacing within six months, there's rust starting under that scrape, and the service book stops in 2021."

"My dad had it serviced. He just didn't stamp the book."

"Then your dad's not here, and the book is." She folded her arms. "Thirty-three. Cash. Today."

Neil looked at the car, then at the house behind him, where his mother, Ruth, was watching from the kitchen window with a mug in her hands. He had told her he'd get at least four thousand. He had told himself he'd get forty-two.

"Forty," he tried.

"Thirty-four, and I'll take the roof rack off your hands."

"The roof rack's worth two hundred on its own."

"Then thirty-four, and you keep it."

Neil's shoulders dropped. He held out the keys. Gloria counted out the notes on the bonnet, and Neil kept the roof rack, which he had no use for at all.

"Is that him?" She pointed. On page four was a photograph: the same man, the same stained jacket, standing in a flooded farmyard ten kilometres downstream. Volunteer from across the border helps families after the river burst, said the caption. His name was Tomas Dvořák.

The dark stains were mud.

On Thursday, Tomas came in for more batteries. Werner rang them up, then added a box of coffee to the bag and waved away the money.

Zara Pemberton arrived on a Monday in green trainers and asked what everything was. Not in a polite way. In a way that meant she wanted to know.

"That's a Heidelberg platen," I told her. "Older than your parents."

"Can I touch it?"

"Not until Thursday."

On Tuesday she swept the floor without being asked and found a brass sort that had been missing since 1998, a lowercase g. I pretended it was nothing. I put it in my pocket and, later, back in its drawer where it belonged.

On Wednesday Mr. Edwin Gresham, whose grandfather hired me, sent her to the office to learn the invoices. By noon she was back in the press room, finished. "They were all the same," she said. "I made a spreadsheet." Edwin looked at it for a long time and then asked her to make another.

On Thursday I let her set a line of type. She did it backwards first, like everyone does, and swore under her breath, like everyone does. The second time she got it right. We printed it on cream card: WELCOME, ZARA.

On Friday she asked whether I might teach her properly. Not for the internship. For after.

I told her I would think about it. I, Bernard Hulme, seventy-one years old, have been thinking about nothing else all weekend.

The argument happened, as most Delgado arguments did, over Sunday lasagne.

"He backed into the Hendersons' mailbox, Mike," said Teresa. "Twice."

"Once," said Frank Delgado, eighty-four, from the head of the table. "The second time the mailbox moved."

Mike, his son, put down his fork. "Pop drove a bus for thirty years. He's got more road sense than you and me put together."

"He drove a bus in 1985."

"I'm right here," Frank said, but they talked over him the way people talk over a radio.

His granddaughter Lucia, seventeen, who had got her licence in June, said nothing. After dessert, Frank tossed her the keys to his Buick. "Come on. You drive. I want to see how they teach it now."

They went out along Route 9 with the windows down. Lucia drove carefully, both hands on the wheel, eyes everywhere. At the light by the old feed store, Frank said quietly, "I didn't see that cyclist last week. Over on Elm. Didn't see him at all until he shouted."

Lucia glanced at him. "Did you tell Mom?"

"I'm telling you." He watched the fields go by. "Your grandmother used to say I'd know when. I suppose I do."

When they got home, Teresa and Mike were still at the table, bus timetables spread between them. Frank set the Buick's keys down in the middle of it all.

"Lucia drives me to bingo on Thursdays," he announced. "And to the cemetery on Sundays. That's settled."

Nobody argued. Lucia picked up the keys.

"I want to be at the top," she told her friends over pizza. "Sitting at the top. You know what I mean."

Ivy Marsh, who had climbed half the Munros, had her laptop open before the pizza was finished. By midnight she had found a charity that lent out off-road trail chairs: one fat wheel, a seat, and handles front and back like a rickshaw. Sam Pryce, who rowed, volunteered for the back handles. His boyfriend, Bastian, volunteered for the front and immediately regretted it.

They set off at six on a clear June morning. Ray had insisted on one rule: she would push her own wheelchair on the flat sections, and nobody was allowed to say "you're doing amazing." The first two miles were gravel track, and she wheeled them, forearms burning, ahead of all three of them.

Then the path turned to rock and heather. Ray transferred to the trail chair, and the real work began. She leaned into the turns to keep it balanced; Sam and Bastian pushed and lifted and swore; Ivy scouted ahead and shouted back where the boulders hid.

At the false summit, Bastian lay flat in the grass and announced that he was dying. Ray threw a flapjack at him.

They reached the cairn at two. The whole valley lay below, her town a scatter of grey roofs. Ray found her own street, then her own window.

"There," she said. "That's where I watched from."

Nobody said amazing. Nobody needed to.

Premise: A blind musician auditions for an orchestra.
text:
The Halsworth Philharmonic held its auditions behind a screen, so that the panel would judge only the sound. Tomás Ferreira found this very funny.

"Everyone's blind today," he told his guide dog, Pip, in the corridor. Pip thumped her tail against the radiator.

The stage manager, a brisk woman named Corinne, guided him to the chair by the elbow and moved the music stand aside without being asked. Tomás had learned the excerpts the way he learned everything: by ear, and from Braille scores that his old teacher, Mr. Adebayo, had transcribed for him note by note when he was nine. The Dvořák concerto. The Brahms solo. The fiendish passage from Don Juan that cellists traded horror stories about.

He tuned, breathed, and began.

Behind the screen, the conductor, Ilse Brandt, stopped writing halfway through the Brahms. Beside her, the principal cellist, Martin Leclerc, closed his eyes, which he only did when something was very good or very bad.

The Strauss came off clean. Tomás let the last note ring until the hall swallowed it.

"Thank you, candidate seven," said Ilse. "Please wait outside."

Corinne led him back to Pip. Forty minutes later she came for him again: final round, screen removed. Tomás walked out with Pip at his side and heard, quite distinctly, the whole panel go silent.

"Well," said Martin Leclerc after a moment. "That explains how you play without watching your bow."

"I've never watched my bow," said Tomás. "Shall I play the Dvořák again?"

He got the job on Thursday.

In March, a bug in the motor controller had the whole team stumped. Hana found it in an oscilloscope trace that everyone else had skimmed past.

"How did you see that?" Lior signed, clumsily.

She grinned. "I look."

Her neighbour on the staircase was Hugo Ashworth-Fane, who had been to the same school as two prime ministers and was mildly embarrassed about it. He knocked on her door that first night holding a bottle of wine and no corkscrew.

"I don't suppose—"

Jade had a corkscrew. Jade had a corkscrew, a sewing kit, plasters, a torch and a multi-tool, because Sharon had worked nights for twenty years and believed in being ready.

At formal hall there were three forks. Jade watched Hugo and copied him. Hugo, she noticed, was watching someone else.

Her first tutorial was with Dr. Imogen Penrose, who handed back her essay on Milton covered in red ink. Jade went cold. Then she read the comments. Original. Argue this harder. Where did you learn to think like this?

Stretford library, she wanted to say. The one with the broken heating, from age nine until it shut.

That night she rang her mum from the bench by the lodge, because the signal on her staircase was dreadful.

"Is it posh?" said Sharon.

"Dead posh," said Jade. "Mum, I think I'm good at this."

"Course you are," said Sharon. "Have you eaten the corned beef?"

At 9:47 p.m., between the fourteenth and fifteenth floors of Hale Tower, the lift shuddered and stopped.

Victoria Hale, whose name was on the building, pressed the alarm button three times. Then she pressed every other button.

"It won't help," said the man beside her. He wore a grey uniform, and a mop and a yellow bucket stood at his feet. "Happens once a month. The engineer takes about an hour."

"An hour."

"Fifty minutes, if it's Terry on call."

She looked at him properly for the first time. Sixties, reading glasses on a cord, a badge that said ADE. "You've been stuck before."

"Four times. I'm Ade Balogun. I do floors twelve to twenty."

She sat down on the floor of the lift, in her good suit, because her knees had begun to shake. Ade noticed and did not mention it. Instead he told her about the fourteenth floor, where the accounts team stacked their coffee cups into a pyramid every Friday, and about the nineteenth, where someone in legal kept a goldfish nobody admitted to owning, which Ade had been feeding since March.

"You know more about my company than I do," Victoria said.

"I see it at night. It's a different company at night."

He told her about his daughter, studying medicine in Leeds, and Victoria told him, surprising herself, about her father, who had started the firm with one van.

At 10:41 the lift jolted upward. Terry had been quick.

The doors opened on fifteen. Victoria stood, brushed off her skirt, and paused.

"The goldfish," she said. "What's its name?"

"Chairman," said Ade.

Eli Navarro told Kofi first, because Kofi had been his best friend since they were six and had once eaten a worm on Eli's behalf.

They were on the roof of Kofi's garage, where they weren't supposed to be. Eli had practised the sentence for a month. It came out as: "I think I like boys. I mean, I do. Like boys."

Kofi Mensah considered this for a long moment, chewing a blade of grass. "Is it Marcus from chemistry?"

"No!" Then: "Maybe. Shut up."

"Everyone likes Marcus from chemistry," said Kofi. "Even I like Marcus from chemistry." He bumped Eli's shoulder. "Okay. Cool. Is that it? You looked like you were going to tell me you were dying."

Telling his parents was harder, because there was no roof and no grass, only the kitchen table and the smell of his father's onions burning.

His mother, Lucía, put down her tea. His father, Roberto, turned off the gas, which he never did mid-cooking.

"Mamá. Papá. I'm gay."

The silence lasted three seconds. Eli counted.

Then his father said, "Okay," in a voice that cracked in the middle, and came round the table and held him, smelling of onions. His mother was crying, which Eli hadn't expected, until she said, "I was so afraid you'd never tell us. I was afraid you thought you couldn't."

Afterwards his father went back to the onions. They were ruined. He made them again.

Later, Eli texted Kofi: Told them. It's okay.

Kofi sent back a single worm emoji.

Simon passed the container round. By the time it came back it was empty, and Brenda had written his husband's name, Tunde, on a napkin with her phone number underneath.

Bernadette Pugh interviewed at two. She was heavyset, with a pockmarked complexion and thick glasses she kept pushing up her nose. Martin caught himself checking his watch at minute twelve. When she paused over the same budget question, he wrote "hesitant" in the margin.

His co-panellist, Yolanda Ferris, had been quiet all day. Afterwards, she slid her scoresheet across the desk.

"I used the rubric," she said. "Same five questions, scored before I looked up. Bernadette answered the forecasting question better. She just took longer to start. Sienna never actually answered it."

Martin looked down at his own notes. Nerves, totally understandable. Hesitant.

He read them again. Then he picked up the phone and invited both women back for a second round: a written case exercise, names removed, marked by Yolanda and someone from finance who had never seen either face.

Bernadette's answer was sharper and more detailed, and it caught an error in the sample data that the finance team had missed for a year.

She started in October. Martin kept the two notes, nerves and hesitant, pinned above his desk.

Premise: An overweight person joins a gym for the first time.
text:
Gemma Halloran sat in the car park of IronWorks Gym for twenty-five minutes before she went in, rehearsing reasons to drive away.

Inside it was loud and bright and smelled of rubber. The girl at the front desk, Tasha, had a nose ring and a clipboard and looked only at Gemma's face. "First time? Brilliant. Want the tour, or want to be left alone?"

"Left alone," said Gemma. "Then maybe the tour."

She found a treadmill in the corner, facing a wall, and walked for eleven minutes before her shins began to complain. Her reflection in the mirror opposite was red and damp, and she looked away from it.

Next to her, an old man in a faded Seoul Marathon 1988 T-shirt was walking at exactly the same speed.

"Pak," he said, nodding. "Seventy-six years old. Knee replacements, both sides. My granddaughter makes me come."

"Gemma. My doctor makes me come."

"Doctors and granddaughters," said Mr. Pak. "Very bossy."

They walked side by side for twenty minutes. He told her about the marathon. She told him about her job at the council, and the stairs at the office she'd started avoiding.

When she finally stopped, legs trembling, Tasha came over with a paper cup of water. "Twenty-nine minutes," she said. "That's good for day one. That's good for anyone."

Gemma came back on Thursday. Mr. Pak was on the same treadmill, and he had saved the one beside him with his towel.

By March she was taking the office stairs again, all four flights. On Fridays she took the last one two at a time, just because she could.

Arthur Penhallow was found on Tuesday morning at the foot of the stairs in his antique shop on Quay Street, among the shards of a Ming vase that had not, it turned out, been Ming. Detective Inspector Odile Brannock arrived at nine. She was a broad, solid woman of fifty with cropped grey hair, a raincoat two sizes too big that had belonged to her late husband, and a face that looked permanently on the verge of disbelief. She looked at the body, then at the stairs, then at the banister.

"He didn't fall," she told Constable Hughes. "Someone's wiped this rail. Old men hold on to rails."

The nephew, Julian Penhallow, came to the station of his own accord. He was thirty-five and handsome in a soft, well-tended way: honey-coloured hair, a navy cashmere jumper, a wristwatch that cost more than the constable earned in a year. His eyes were grey and very steady, and he cried at exactly the right moments.

"Uncle Arthur was everything to me," he said.

Odile nodded and slid a photograph across the table: the shop's fake Ming, insured for forty thousand pounds the previous week, with Julian's signature on the policy.

Julian's steady grey eyes moved, just once, towards the door.

"Sit down, Mr. Penhallow," said Odile. "We'll be a while."

Dr. Mei-Lin Zhao was already in the corridor with a radiation kit, counting out iodine tablets.

The navigator, Teodoro Vance, pulled up their trajectory and went pale. "Without thrust we miss Callisto orbit. Next stop is Jupiter. In about nineteen hours."

Security Chief Ana Sokolova, who was six foot two and had never been inside the crawlspace because she didn't fit, said, "Who's small enough?"

Everyone turned to look at Bartholomew Quill, the cook, who was five foot four and holding a spatula.

"Oh," said Barty. "Oh, no."

He went in anyway, in a suit two sizes too big, with Rurik talking him through every bolt and Ana holding his safety line. Dr. Zhao watched his dosimeter tick upward. It took forty minutes. He came out shaking and grey and grinning.

The engine coughed, then caught, then roared.

Teodoro plotted a new burn. Adaeze logged it.

Barty, released from the medical bay at noon, made pancakes for everyone and refused to discuss it.

Premise: A lighthouse keeper during the worst storm in a decade.
text:
The storm hit Skerrow Light at dusk, and by nine o'clock Isobel Garrow had stopped pretending it was an ordinary one.

The wind came off the Atlantic at ninety knots. Spray reached the gallery, a hundred and twelve feet up, and slid down the lantern glass like hands. The tower, which had stood since 1851, made a low groaning sound Isobel had heard only once before, the winter her father kept the light and she was a girl hiding under the kitchen table.

At 10:20 the power went.

The beam died mid-sweep. Below, the radio crackled: the coastguard at Stornoway, Neil Frazer, his voice thin. "Skerrow, we've got the Morning Star out of Ullapool, skipper Donal Mackie, three crew. Engine trouble. They're looking for your light."

Isobel didn't answer. She was already climbing.

The generator in the base had flooded. The old clockwork mechanism, kept polished for the museum people, had not. She cranked the weight up by hand, arms burning, lit the backup lamp, and pushed the great lens round until the gears caught.

The light swept out again. Slower, heavier, like breathing.

Every forty minutes she wound it. Every forty minutes her hands bled a little more. At 2:15 the radio spoke again.

"Skerrow, Morning Star. We see you. We see you. Coming round the north side now."

Isobel sat down on the iron stair and laughed until she cried.

At dawn the storm blew itself out over Lewis. At noon Donal Mackie came up the path with a bottle of whisky and three soaked crewmen behind him, and all four of them shook her ruined hands very gently.

Premise: A robot learns to paint.
text:
The robot's designation was KR-7, but Bettina Lorenz called it Kay, because she was eighty-one and did not have time for numbers.

Her grandson, Anton, had bought Kay to help her around the flat after her fall: lifting, cleaning, reminding her about pills. He had not expected it to stand in the doorway of her studio for an hour on its second day, watching her mix ochre.

"You may ask," Bettina said, without turning round.

"What are you making?"

"Wrong question. Ask what I'm looking at."

Kay considered. "The window. The pear tree. The light on the pear tree."

"Good. Now you paint it."

Its first painting was perfect. Every leaf exact, every shadow measured to the millimetre. Bettina looked at it for a long time.

"It's a photograph," she said. "Do it again. This time, paint only what you noticed first."

Kay painted for three weeks. It painted the pear tree a hundred and six times. The leaves grew looser. The colours drifted. One morning it painted only the light: a smear of yellow against blue, and nothing else.

Bettina put on her glasses. "Why yellow?"

"At 7:12 this morning, the sun reached the tree, and you said 'Ah.' I did not have a better way to record it."

She was quiet. Then she took the canvas and hung it beside her own, on the wall above the stove where the good paintings went.

When Anton visited on Sunday, he found the two of them side by side at the easel, arguing about cadmium red.

Premise: A lost dog finds its way home across a city.
text:
Juno, a scruffy brown terrier with one ear up and one ear down, slipped her lead outside the vet's on Carver Street when a lorry backfired, and by the time Colin Greenleaf had stopped shouting her name, she was six streets away and entirely lost.

The city was enormous and smelled of everything. Juno ran until her legs shook, then sat under a bus shelter and thought, in the way dogs think, about home: the creak of the back gate, the smell of Hattie's trainers, the river.

The river. Home was near the river. And the river, she knew somewhere deep in her nose, was downhill.

She went downhill.

She crossed the market, where a fishmonger named Sal tossed her a sardine head and said, "Go on, then." She followed a jogger along the canal for a mile because he smelled faintly of the park near her house. She waited at a crossing beside an old woman, Mrs. Odette Bellweather, who said, "Wait for the green man, dear," and Juno, who had no idea what that meant, waited anyway and crossed when everyone else did.

At dusk she found the river. The smell of it was right. She turned left, and there was the bakery, and the bridge, and the corner where Hattie waited for the school bus.

Hattie Greenleaf, nine, had been sitting on the front step since four o'clock with a tin of sausages and a handmade sign that said LOST: JUNO. ONE EAR UP. She saw the dog first. She dropped the sign.

Colin, inside on the phone to the council, heard the shriek and ran out to find his daughter flat on the pavement, laughing, being licked half to death.

Juno had a bath that night, which she considered deeply unfair.

"No," Dev agreed. "But I've watched him breathe all night. He's not the patient you're describing."

Ingrid's jaw tightened. She hated being contradicted by anyone, and she hated it more when they might be right. She also remembered a man in her second year of residency, dead because everyone had been polite and waited.

"Repeat the lactate," she said at last. "And get me a CT. If either looks wrong, he goes up."

She almost smiled. "Wake me if his belly changes. Even slightly."

"Both mothers?"

Daniel considered. "It gets quieter. You learn to carry it more carefully."

"I'm sixty-one, Daniel. I'm still carrying it badly."

"You asked the jury twice if they needed more time. You allowed both families a statement. I wouldn't call that badly."

She looked at him and for a moment saw her own younger self. "Thank you."

At two o'clock, the courtroom rose. Daniel stood by the bench, ready with the papers. The foreperson, a retired teacher named Mrs. Lindqvist, handed up the form, and her hand trembled.

Margaret read it once, silently, and breathed. Then she raised her eyes and, in a steady voice, began to speak.

Twelve-year-old Kaito Morimoto had already climbed three rocks and a fallen birch before he noticed the path was gone. "Come on, Hana! There's a shortcut!"

His younger sister, ten-year-old Hana, stayed where she was, clutching the straps of her backpack. "Kaito, we're supposed to stay on the trail."

"What trail? Trails are for people who are scared."

"I'm not scared," Hana said, in a small voice. "I'm careful."

He plunged ahead, crashing through ferns, and she followed because she could not bear to be left. An hour later, the afternoon light had turned orange, and neither of them recognised anything.

"We're lost," Hana whispered. "I told you."

"We're not lost. We're exploring."

But when the first owl called, even Kaito flinched. He stopped, panting, and for the first time looked uncertain.

Hana knelt and studied the ground. "Look. Moss grows on the north side of the trunks. And I've been counting our turns. We came down the hill, so the road is uphill, behind us."

"You were counting?"

"Somebody had to."

They climbed. When branches snagged her sleeve, Hana cried quietly but kept walking. When a hollow in the dark scared her, Kaito marched in front, loudly singing to chase away bears. At last, they saw the headlamps of the search party and heard their father, Daisuke, shouting their names.

Kaito squeezed her hand. "You're the best navigator."

"You're the best bear-scarer," Hana said, and sobbed with relief.

Premise: A couple breaks up in a cafe; describe how each of them handles it in the days after.
text:
In the corner of Café Marlow, Elena Voss stirred her cold coffee and said, "I think we want different things." Across the table, Jonah Bright nodded as if she had read him a weather report. Neither cried. They split the bill, and Jonah walked her to the tram.

Elena handled the following days by keeping busy. On Monday she reorganised her whole flat. On Tuesday she signed up for a pottery class she had been postponing for two years. By Thursday she had fixed the squeaky door, repainted the hallway, and told her sister Camille she was "completely fine." Camille, who knew her well, simply came over with wine and sat on the freshly painted floor until Elena's voice cracked.

"I'm so tired," she said.

"I know," said Camille. "Stop fixing things."

Jonah did the opposite. For three days he did nothing. He cancelled a client call, lay on his couch, and replayed the café in his head, wondering if he should have argued. He ate crackers for dinner. On Friday his friend Tariq turned up with a bag of groceries and a cheap bottle of whisky.

"You look terrible."

"I feel fine."

"You're lying on a couch in the dark, man."

Jonah let out a breath that turned into a laugh and then into something else, and Tariq sat down beside him without a word.

On Sunday, Elena's clay bowl came out of the kiln, lopsided. Jonah finally opened the curtains. Neither knew yet that the other had survived the week.

The Honda Civic sat in Mr. Raymond Kowalski's driveway with a sign on the windshield: $6,500. Dina Haddad walked a slow circle around it while Raymond, sixty and square-shouldered, leaned on the garage door with folded arms.

"Seventy thousand miles," Dina said. "But there's a scratch on the bumper and the tyres are worn."

"Six-five," said Raymond. "Firm."

"I was thinking five thousand."

"Not happening." He didn't blink. "There's a guy coming at four who's already offered six."

Dina's boyfriend, Marcus, lingered by the mailbox, picking at a loose thread on his sleeve. He had come along to help, but he had always been bad at confrontation. At a restaurant, he'd once eaten an undercooked burger rather than complain.

"What about fifty-five hundred?" Dina asked.

"Sixty-two."

"Fifty-seven."

"Sixty-one."

She glanced at Marcus, who gave the smallest nod, wanting this to be over. Dina frowned.

"Marcus, go sit in the car."

"Which car?"

"Mine."

He went. She turned back. "Mr. Kowalski, the brakes will need changing within a year. That's four hundred dollars. I'll do fifty-eight and not a cent more."

Raymond studied her for a long moment. Then his arms dropped. "You drive a hard bargain, miss."

"Fifty-eight?"

"Fifty-eight."

They shook. Later, Marcus murmured, "I would have paid six-five."

"I know," said Dina, grinning, and handed him the keys.

At one o'clock, as clouds slid over the peaks, she said simply, "Time."

Nobody argued. They turned together and started down, and halfway back, Tomasz said, "I'd follow Anya anywhere."

"Even into a sandbox?" Beatrice asked.

"Yes."

"I like it." Dolores opened the door wider. "Tell your husband the gutters on that house are a disgrace. I've been telling the landlord for years."

Yuki laughed, delighted. By Saturday, Gabriel had lent Hiroshi a ladder, Sora was riding bikes with the Torres boys, and Dolores had invited Emi inside to see her collection of porcelain cats. Birch Lane, which had been watching, was suddenly in the middle of things.

Ruzena Horakova had run the hardware shop in the border town of Nagy Verke for thirty years, and she knew every face on the street. So when a tall man in a grey coat stepped through the door on a wet November afternoon, speaking with an accent she couldn't place, she felt her shoulders stiffen.

"Good afternoon. I need a long rope, please. Twenty metres. And a hatchet."

Ruzena slid the hatchet's price tag out of sight. "What for?"

"For my grandfather's orchard. Trees have fallen."

"Which orchard?"

He smiled, puzzled. "Near the hill road. He is Mr. Bela Szabo."

Ruzena froze. Bela Szabo was her oldest friend's brother, and he had been dead two years. The orchard was now owned by a grandson she'd never met.

"You're the grandson?"

"Yes. Matyas. I grew up in Toronto. My mother spoke only English, so my Hungarian is poor." He laughed, embarrassed. "I came to take care of the land."

Ruzena put the hatchet down. She had been standing like a guard behind a wall, and she felt foolish. "I knew your grandfather. He bought nails from me every spring. Forty years."

"I know. He talked about you in his letters."

"Did he?"

"He said the woman at the hardware shop was the only honest person in the valley."

Ruzena looked at the shelf, blinked hard, and reached for the rope. "Twenty metres. First one is free. Welcome home."

The night train from Vienna to Venice was nearly empty, so the three travellers in compartment seven had each assumed they would have it to themselves.

"Is this seat taken?" Paulo asked, in three languages, none of them well.

"Take it," said Sigrid, not looking up from her knitting.

An hour later, the compartment lights dimmed, the train hummed through the Alps, and Kwame offered ginger tea. Paulo, who had never had it, coughed theatrically and then asked for more.

"What are you knitting?" Kwame asked.

"A scarf for my sister. Though she'll say it's too long."

"Is it?"

"It's three metres."

Paulo burst out laughing, and from the guitar case he drew out a small, worn instrument and played a bossa nova so soft it barely rose above the sound of the wheels. Sigrid's needles slowed. Kwame closed his book.

By two in the morning, all three were asleep, Sigrid's scarf draped over Paulo's knees as a blanket. At dawn, they woke to a grey lagoon and a city floating on water, and none of them wanted the ride to end.

At Atlantic Avenue, he stopped. The fare was nineteen dollars. She handed him thirty.

"Too much," Oumar said.

"Tell Awa to study hard." Samira stepped out into the rain. "Tell her a nurse said it's worth it."

"And now?"

"Now I do the stairs twice a day and complain about my knees." She grinned. "You're doing fine. Come on Thursday. I'll show you the good machines."

Nell led the children in singing to keep them calm.

Below, in the cottage, his granddaughter Wren, twelve, was making cocoa and pretending not to be afraid. She had come for the summer and stayed through the autumn, and he had never been so glad of anything.

At midnight, the radio crackled. "Mayday, mayday, this is the trawler Mary Constance..."

Thaddeus seized the handset. "Skerry Point here. What's your position?"

"Two miles south-west. Engine's failed. We're being pushed onto the reef."

He looked out. The reef was invisible. "Wren!" he called down. "Bring the signal lamp. I need you to flash their name."

She climbed up, soaked, and together, with cold fingers, they sent the beam in long and short pulses toward the trawler. Hours passed. At dawn, the Mary Constance limped past the point, her captain, Odalys Ferreira, waving from the deck.

Wren leaned against her grandfather, shivering. "Did we do it?"

"We did it." Thaddeus put his arm around her. "That's what the light is for."

The robot, whose maker had named it Pip, had spent four years sorting packages in a warehouse in Rotterdam, until the night shift supervisor, Annelies de Vries, found it standing motionless before a vending machine's glowing panel.

A warehouse engineer named Joost noticed it. "It's learning to paint."

"It's learning to see," said Annelies.

Over the months, Pip's squares became windows, then trees, then a portrait of Annelies, whose crooked smile it rendered in four careful yellow strokes. When she saw it, she turned away to hide her face.

"Is it good?" Pip asked.

"It's you," she said finally. "The way you see us. Slow, and kind, and a little bit wrong."

Pip considered this. "May I paint another?"

"Please."

On the wall of the warehouse breakroom, an exhibition began. Its first sign, in Joost's handwriting, read: By Pip. Still learning.

"No," she said. "I have you, and eleven other cousins I'm very fond of, and a garden I love. I have a good life, Daniel. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise."

A child in the balcony asked a question that was not on the programme, and the hall laughed warmly.

She closed by saying that science was not a single flash of genius but a long line of people refusing to give up on a small, stubborn fact. Then she stepped back, the applause rose again, and Tomas, still holding his sign, wiped his eyes.

The first showed a news channel reporting a data breach that had exposed the bank details of forty thousand customers. The second showed the share price, down eleven percent before nine. The third showed an email from the board chair, Patricia Lowe, asking him to come to a meeting at ten and bring his resignation letter, just in case.

His assistant, Janet Ferris, brought him coffee he did not drink. She had worked for him for nineteen years and had never once seen him look afraid.

"They want a scapegoat," Janet said quietly. "They want somebody to blame, and it isn't going to be the IT department."

Richard knew she was right. The breach had come through a contractor he had hired against the advice of his own security chief, a man named Marcus Vale, who had resigned in March and had not been replaced. Richard had signed off on the cost savings himself, proud of the spreadsheet.

At ten he walked into the boardroom and listened as Patricia read the figures aloud. He did not argue. He admitted the mistake, named Marcus Vale as the man who had warned him, and asked the board to give the security team the budget they had been denied. One director, Gordon Hale, said that was not how a chief executive was supposed to behave.

"No," Richard said. "But it's how I'm going to behave today."

He left the meeting without the letter in his pocket. Janet was waiting in the corridor, and for the first time in nineteen years, she took his hand.

Premise: A child prodigy amazes the adults around them.
text:
At four years old, Lena Park could hear a wrong note from the next room. Her mother, Sarah, was overwhelmed. She had grown up in a flat above a launderette in Leeds and had never imagined her daughter would be turning the heads of professors. Her father, David, an electrician, simply shook his head and said his daughter was probably a little bit magic.

The adults kept coming. A music teacher from the conservatory offered free lessons. A reporter asked for an interview. A neighbour asked whether Lena could play at her wedding. Lena watched each of them with a gravity that made the grown-ups uneasy, as if she were the one assessing them.

At home she played the piano in her pyjamas before school, and once corrected her grandfather's lullaby in the middle of a verse. Min-jun laughed and asked her not to correct his singing in front of the neighbours. Lena told him she would keep her corrections for the piano, which she agreed was far more important.

Sarah began to worry. She asked the conservatory whether her daughter could still have a childhood. The director, a stern woman named Helen Marsh, looked at Lena for a long moment and said that some children needed to be allowed to be children, and that the piano would wait for them if it was meant to be theirs.

That night Lena fell asleep on the sofa with her head on her grandfather's knee while the radio played a slow song she had never heard before. In the morning she could already hum it.

"Is he okay?" asked the woman across the aisle, Ruth Abbott, a retired schoolteacher with a shopping bag on her knees.

"He's not," Marcus said, and was already on his knees in the gangway.

The man, who had given his name as Gerald Okonkwo when he boarded at the last station, had no pulse. Marcus began compressions while Ruth shouted for help. The conductor, a young man named Tariq Hassan, ran down the carriage and radioed ahead. Two students in the next seats were already filming, and Marcus told them sharply to put their phones away and fetch the defibrillator from the cabinet by the toilets.

Marcus counted the compressions out loud. He felt ribs give under his hands and kept going. Ruth held Gerald's head steady and talked to him softly, as though he could hear. Tariq returned with the defibrillator, and Marcus delivered the first shock as the train slowed into Penrith station.

Nothing. Then, after the second shock, a shudder and a thin breath. Gerald's eyes flickered open and fixed on Marcus's face.

The ambulance crew met the train on the platform. The doctor on board said the next ten minutes had been critical, and that the man would live. Gerald, still grey and shaking, asked Marcus for his name. Marcus told him, then sat down on the platform bench and let Ruth hand him a cup of tea from the station kiosk, his own hands trembling now that the work was over.

Premise: A villain explains their plan to the hero.
text:
The control room beneath the Thornfield Estate was colder than Ada Reyes had expected, and the man at the central console was smiling as though they were old friends. Dr. Sebastian Crane had once taught her chemistry at the academy. Now he had a thousand litres of nerve agent sealed in a tank beneath the city's water main, and a timer counting down on the wall.

"You've come a long way, Ada," he said. "I always said you would."

She kept her hand near the holster on her hip. Behind her, Officer Dev Patel stood guard at the lift with his rifle pointed at the floor, the way he had been trained.

"Why?" Ada asked.

Crane laughed. He explained that the city had sold its water contracts to a consortium that had been quietly poisoning the poor districts for years, through lead pipes and falsified reports. He had gathered the evidence. The courts had ignored it. The newspapers had been bought.

"So you'll poison everyone instead," Ada said.

"Not everyone. Only the people who signed the contracts. The release will flood the pumping station at Westgate, and the water will reach only the boardrooms." He tapped the console. "I've been very careful."

Ada noticed the sweat on his forehead and the tremor in his left hand. She noticed the timer was counting down to 2:03, not 2:00. She noticed that his voice had grown quieter.

"You're not sure, are you," she said. "You're not sure the water will stop where you want it to."

Crane's smile faltered. Behind her, Dev stepped forward without being asked, and the room became very quiet, with only the timer ticking.

"You'd be brilliant with children," Ian said.

"You'd be brilliant with coffee," Grace said. "Give it up."

He laughed, and she laughed, and for a moment the tension of the night dropped away. Then her pager buzzed on her belt. Ian stubbed out the cigarette on the concrete ledge and dropped the stub into the little tin he kept for the purpose.

They went down the stairs together. At the bottom, Grace paused and touched his arm. "Thank you," she said. "For the break."

"Anytime," said Ian, and meant it.

Premise: A boss dictates a letter to a secretary.
text:
Gerald Finch had dictated letters for thirty years, and in all that time he had never once paused to ask whether his secretary was writing down the right words. Miriam Holt sat across the desk with her pencil poised over her notepad, her spectacles low on her nose, and waited for him to begin.

"To Mr. Alan Ward, Harrowgate Textiles," Gerald said. "Dear Mr. Ward. Further to our telephone conversation of Tuesday, I regret that my firm cannot extend the payment terms you requested."

Miriam wrote it down. She had typed a thousand such letters and knew how Gerald liked his commas. But this morning, as she wrote, she remembered that the telephone conversation had not been on Tuesday at all. She had been in the room. It had been Thursday, and Mr. Ward had cried.

"Mr. Finch," she said carefully, "I believe Mr. Ward's call was on Thursday."

Gerald waved a hand. "Thursday, Tuesday. The man should keep better records."

Miriam hesitated, then kept writing. Gerald went on: the payment terms would remain at thirty days, the company regretted any inconvenience, and Mr. Ward should expect a visit from the collections team in the new year. He did not mention that Mr. Ward's company had supplied the cloth for every uniform Miriam had ever worn in the office.

When the letter was finished, Gerald signed it without reading it. Miriam took the paper, looked at the words for a long moment, then folded it very slowly and slid it into her top drawer, next to the other letters she had written and never sent.

Premise: A programmer fixes a bug at three in the morning.
text:
At 3:14 in the morning, Kofi Mensah had been staring at the same stack trace for three hours. The bug was in the payment reconciliation service, which had worked perfectly for two years and had failed, without warning, at the exact moment the finance team needed it most. His manager, Diane Russo, had already sent four messages asking for an update. His coffee had gone cold beside the keyboard.

He pulled up the logs for the fifth time. The error appeared only for transactions stamped just after midnight in the Pacific time zone, which made no sense, because the service ran in Frankfurt.

Kofi walked to the window. The office was empty except for a cleaner at the far end, pushing a mop across the carpet. The city below was quiet.

He went back to his desk and searched the codebase for the word "timezone". Four hundred and twelve results. He read through them slowly, one by one, the way his grandmother had taught him to read a recipe. Near the bottom of the list, in a file written by a colleague named Priya Shah who had left the company in May, he found a conversion function that assumed every day had twenty-four hours.

It was an old assumption, and an easy one to miss. The clocks had changed the weekend before, and the function had never been updated.

Kofi fixed it in eleven lines. He wrote a test that would have caught it, ran the suite, and watched the green ticks appear down the screen. He sent Diane a short message: "Found it. Timezone conversion. Fix is in review." Then he picked up the cold coffee, drank it anyway, and went to find something to eat.

Jade went to Clara's house for a birthday party and was surprised by how quiet it was, with so many rooms and nobody in most of them.

Mrs. Whitfield noticed the friendship and felt uneasy. Mrs. Dunmore noticed it too, and felt proud and afraid. Neither mother mentioned it. But on the last day of term the two girls sat together on the Dunmores' back wall, swinging their legs, and planned the summer as though the top of the hill and the bottom of the street were the same place.

Edith Morrow was eighty-one, and on the morning of her birthday she stared at the box on the kitchen table as though it might bite. Her grandchildren, Ben and Tilly, had chosen it, paid for it with their pocket money, and presented it with such enthusiasm that she could not refuse.

"It's a telephone that does everything," Tilly said, pulling the plastic off the screen.

"I have a telephone," Edith said. "It rings. I answer it."

Ben sat beside her and patiently showed her how to turn the thing on. The screen lit up with a photograph of a mountain that Ben had chosen as her wallpaper. Edith squinted at it, then at the strange little icons along the bottom, each as mysterious as a letter from a foreign government.

It took three weeks. She learned to photograph the garden and send the pictures to her sister in Yorkshire with a message that said only "Look at the roses." She learned to send Ben a short message every morning and wait, with a fluttering heart, for his reply of a single thumbs-up. She learned to ask the device for the weather, which answered in the voice of a polite young man.

Then one evening Tilly rang her from the next room, and Edith heard her granddaughter's voice coming out of the little box, clear as a bell. She laughed out loud and called back, "Hello, darling," and Tilly called back, "Nan, you're on speaker. You're not supposed to shout."

By summer Edith had stopped asking for help with every button. She had joined a video call with her sister, shown off her garden to the camera, and once accidentally filmed the kitchen ceiling for an entire afternoon. Ben said it was the best birthday present he had ever given anyone. Edith said that was ridiculous, and that she would give him a proper present next year, one that did not need charging.

Premise: A mechanic and a hairdresser run shops on the same street and help each other during a storm.
text:
Tony Russo had run Russo Motors on Dorset Street for twenty-six years, and in all that time he had never once been on speaking terms with the hairdresser across the road, Lupe Garza, who had opened her salon, Curl Up and Dye, the year his divorce came through. They had shouted at each other about parking spaces and argued about the bins. Tony thought her window display was an insult to proper cars. Lupe thought his radio was a crime against the ears.

Then a storm came in on a Friday night in October. The wind tore a sign off the bakery and sent it spinning down the street. Water poured through the gap under Russo Motors' roller door, and the power failed across the whole block.

Tony was in the workshop with a torch in his teeth when he heard banging on the shutter. It was Lupe, soaked to the skin, holding a box of candles and her ten-year-old nephew, Diego, by the collar.

"Your roof's leaking into my back room," she shouted. "Are you going to stand there, or are you going to help?"

Tony helped. They dragged buckets across the floor and rolled old tarpaulins over the sagging ceiling. Diego held the torch while Tony wrestled a stuck drain cover free. By midnight they were sitting on upturned crates in the workshop, sharing a flask of Lupe's terrible instant coffee and the last of a packet of biscuits.

"I thought you hated me," Tony said.

"I do hate your radio," Lupe said. "I don't hate you."

The storm passed by dawn. In the morning Tony found a tin of paint on his doorstep, with a note in Lupe's bold handwriting: "Your sign is crooked. Fix it, or I will." He fixed it. Two days later she came over with a set of spanners she had bought for him, because she had seen his old ones splitting in the rain.

Owen fetched the sketchbook. The drawings were astonishing: a swallow in flight, a fox asleep in the roots of an oak, a clock with its hands melting into roses. Carol turned the pages slowly. David, leaning over her shoulder, went very quiet.

"These are good," David said at last, in the voice of a man surprised by his own honesty. "Really good. But you need to be able to pay the rent while you learn."

"I know," Owen said. "That's why I'm going to be the best apprentice Black Lotus has ever had."

Carol smiled and passed him the bread. David shook his head but took another slice of lasagne, and later that evening he was found at the kitchen table with a pencil, working out how many sessions a month would cover the rent.

Premise: A couple breaks up in a cafe; describe how each of them handles it in the days after.
text:
Sophie and Daniel had agreed to meet at the cafe on the corner of Hollis Street, where they had their first date three years before, because Sophie said it would be cruel to do it anywhere else. Daniel ordered a flat white he did not drink. Sophie ordered a tea she forgot about. For ten minutes they talked about the weather and the new council bins, and then she told him she wanted to end it.

Daniel did not shout. He nodded slowly, looked out of the window at the rain, and asked if there was anyone else. Sophie said no, and he believed her. He said he had known for a month. He paid for both drinks and walked her to the bus stop with his hands in his pockets, and then he went home and sat in the dark until the streetlights came on.

Sophie went to her sister's flat that night and cried on the bathroom floor. In the morning she woke feeling oddly light, as though she had put down a heavy bag she had been carrying up the stairs for months. She cooked herself an elaborate breakfast, went for a long walk along the canal, and called three friends she had been neglecting. By Friday she had started a new painting, and by Sunday she had apologised to her father for an argument from years ago.

Daniel could not stop replaying the conversation. He went back to the cafe three times that week, sitting at the same table and ordering the same flat white. Premise: A family debates whether an elderly relative should keep driving.
text:
The debate about Grandpa Arthur's driving had been going on for a month, and it reached its peak one Sunday afternoon in the Hendersons' kitchen. Arthur, who was eighty-four and had driven a taxi for forty years, sat at the head of the table pretending he was not listening.

"He backed into the post office wall last Tuesday," said his daughter, Helen. "He said it was the bin's fault."

"It was the bin's fault," Arthur said mildly. "It was in the wrong place."

Helen's husband, Kevin, rubbed his forehead. "The doctor said your reactions are slower. We could ask for a test. There's a driving assessment at the community centre."

"I'm not sitting in a room being insulted by a stranger with a clipboard," Arthur said. "I've driven through three snowstorms and a riot."

Their granddaughter, June, a seventeen-year-old who had just passed her own test, looked up from her phone. "I'll drive you," she offered. "We can go to the market on Saturdays. I'm a good driver, Grandpa. You said so yourself."

Arthur softened. He told her the story of the first time he had taught her to reverse, when she had driven the car straight into a hedge and then laughed until she cried. June grinned at the memory.

Helen was not convinced. "It's not just about the driving. It's about whether he can get himself out of a car when something goes wrong."

Arthur looked at his daughter for a long moment. "Helen," he said, "I've been getting myself out of cars my entire life. I'd like to keep doing it for a while yet."

In the end they agreed on a compromise. June would drive him on Saturdays, Kevin would come along on the motorway trips, and Arthur would take the assessment next spring. He grumbled about it, but he also cut out the leaflet and pinned it to the fridge, where it stayed through the whole winter.

Premise: An office cleaner and the company's chief executive are stuck in a lift together for an hour.
text:
The lift in Carrow Tower had a habit of stopping, but Yvonne Baptiste had ridden it for eleven years without incident. On Wednesday evening, with a mop bucket in one hand and a bag of rubbish in the other, she stepped inside at the ground floor and pressed the button for the basement. The doors closed. The lift lurched, groaned, and stopped between the ninth and tenth floors.

The man standing at the back, in an expensive grey suit, was Adrian Fell, chief executive of the company that owned the building. Yvonne had cleaned his office every night for six years and had never once spoken to him, except to say good evening and step aside.

"Well," Adrian said, looking at his watch. "This is a nuisance."

"It happens," Yvonne said, setting down her bucket. "Usually it's the fourth lift that does it."

They waited. The emergency light flickered. Adrian pressed the intercom and was told the engineer would arrive in forty minutes. He sighed and leaned against the wall. Yvonne sat down on her upturned bucket and began to hum softly, a hymn her mother had sung in the kitchen in Lagos before she moved to London.

After ten minutes, Adrian asked what the song was. Yvonne told him. He said his own grandmother had sung something similar in Yorkshire, though he could not remember the words. She taught him the chorus. He sang it badly, she corrected him, and they both laughed.

Then Adrian began talking about his father, who had worked as a porter at a hospital until his back gave out, and about the company he had built from nothing and how lonely it had become at the top. Yvonne listened. She told him about her two sons, one studying law and one who wanted to be a footballer, and about the night shifts she worked to pay for both.

When the lift finally jolted back to life, Adrian turned to her at the doors. "I'd like to know your name properly," he said. "Not just the one on the rota."

"Yvonne," she said, and picked up her bucket. "Good night, Mr. Fell."

The crew of the Harrow job met for the first time in a cramped room above a dry cleaner's on Kell Street, and within an hour they had each proved they were worth the risk. Vivian Osei, the planner, had the blueprints of the Meridian Savings vault spread across the table, marked with coloured pins and notes in cramped handwriting. She had spent four months walking through the building as a tourist.

Marco Russo was the safecracker. He could open a combination lock with his fingertips and a stethoscope, and he had once, as a joke, opened a fridge in a police station while the officers watched. He sat by the window and listened to every word.

Dex Okafor was the driver. He could take any car off any street in under ninety seconds without scratching the paintwork. He wore sunglasses indoors and said almost nothing.

Ruby Lin was the hacker. Her laptop was covered in stickers from universities she had never attended. She had already disabled the building's alarm system in her head, and she was impatient with anyone who wanted to do it the slow way.

Otis Greaves was the muscle. Huge and gentle, with a voice like a cathedral organ, he kept the others laughing and stopped Ruby from flying off the handle. He also knew the guards by name, and had a plan for each of them.

Vivian tapped the blueprints. "Two hours. Three exits. Nobody gets hurt. We take only what we can carry, and we are gone before the morning shift."

They rehearsed for the rest of the week. On the night of the job the crew moved like clockwork. Ruby cut the power to the third floor. Marco opened the vault in four minutes flat. Otis escorted the night guard to the staff room, apologised for the inconvenience, and offered him a biscuit. Dex waited at the kerb with the engine running.

Forty minutes later they were gone, with a bag of bearer bonds, a single gold ring, and a bruise on Vivian's wrist from a hinge she had not seen. They never spoke of it again.

Premise: A basketball player and a maths prodigy have been best friends since childhood. Describe them and their friendship.

Darius Monroe and Hannah Lim met in a kindergarten sandpit, when she told him his sandcastle was structurally unsound and he told her to mind her own business. By the end of the afternoon they had built a tower together, and by the end of the year they were inseparable.

Darius grew up to be the tallest boy in his school, and then the best basketball player in the county. He dribbled on the playground before breakfast and practised free throws until the lights went out in the gym. His coach called him a natural. His mother called him stubborn. Hannah called him an overgrown puppy and dragged him to the library on Saturday mornings.

Hannah was the maths prodigy. At nine she was reading university textbooks in the back of the car. At eleven she corrected her teacher's arithmetic on a school trip to a science museum. At fourteen she won a national competition and came home with a trophy that she placed on the kitchen windowsill, beside a row of Darius's basketball awards.

They were very different. He thought in shapes and movement, reacting before he had time to think. She thought in patterns, and could spend an hour pacing around a problem until its shape became clear. He laughed at her habit of writing equations on the backs of his hands. She teased him for shouting at the television when his team lost.

When Darius tore his knee in his final year, he was afraid he would lose everything. Hannah sat on his bed every evening for a month, working through problems on a whiteboard while he did his physiotherapy. She told him that all the best proofs were built from small steps, and that the knee would heal the same way.

Years later, when Darius walked onto a professional court for the first time, Hannah sat in the front row, scribbling numbers on her programme. Afterwards she showed him the calculation: the average distance he had covered each game, multiplied by the years they had known each other. He told her it was the stupidest thing he had ever seen. He kept the page in his wallet for the rest of his life.

Premise: Two people negotiate the price of a used car. One is tough, the other gives in.
text:
Ilse Brandt walked into the used-car lot on Mill Road with a folder of printouts, a clipboard, and the expression of a woman who had never once paid the asking price. The car she wanted was a ten-year-old silver Volvo estate with a dented rear door and an engine that purred like a cat. Terry Quill, the owner, had put a price of 4,200 pounds on the windscreen.

"Four thousand," Ilse said, before she had even opened the driver's door.

"Four two," Terry said, tapping the sticker. "It's a good car."

"It's a rust bucket with a good paint job. Your brake pads are worn to the metal, and the service history has a three-year gap. I'll give you three thousand, or I walk."

Terry hesitated. He had bought the car at auction for 2,800 and had hoped to make a little profit. He glanced at the rain clouds gathering over the car park and at the folder under Ilse's arm, and his shoulders dropped.

"Thirty-five hundred," he said. "And you pay cash today."

Ilse shook her head. She did not even look up from the clipboard. "Three thousand. Cash today, and you throw in the rain covers."

Terry sighed heavily, and then, to Ilse's mild astonishment, he agreed. He signed the paperwork with a shaking hand and gave her the keys without another word. Ilse drove the car out of the lot, and as she turned onto Mill Road she saw him in the rear mirror, standing alone in the rain, rubbing his neck and muttering to nobody in particular.

Premise: Three travellers from three different countries share a train compartment overnight. Say where each one is from.
text:
The overnight sleeper from Vienna to Venice had only four berths, and by the time the train left the station three of them were taken by strangers who had not yet decided whether to be friendly. Siobhan Keane, a nurse from Cork in Ireland, took the bunk by the window. Kenji Mori, a software engineer from Osaka in Japan, sat opposite with a laptop he did not open. Lucas Ferreira, a photographer from Curitiba in Brazil, climbed onto the top bunk with his camera bag and a bag of oranges.

The fourth berth stayed empty until midnight, when a trader from Rotterdam in the Netherlands, Pieter Vos, stumbled in apologising about a late connection from Munich.

They did not speak much at first. Then Lucas offered an orange to the room, and Siobhan laughed and said nobody had given her fruit on a train since her grandmother's funeral. Kenji admitted he had been too shy to talk to anyone. Pieter said he had been travelling for three days and had lost all sense of time.

They talked about home. Siobhan described the rain in Cork, which she claimed never stopped. Kenji described the cherry blossoms along the river in Osaka, which he missed every year because he was always working. Lucas talked about the carnival in Curitiba, where people danced until dawn, and Pieter confessed that he had never once danced in his life.

Somewhere past the border the train slowed in the dark, and they all went quiet. Lucas photographed the sleeping city lights through the window. Siobhan drew a little map on the steamed glass with her fingertip. Kenji wrote down the names of the stations in katakana, to remember them later.

By dawn they had exchanged addresses, promised to meet in Venice for coffee, and agreed on one thing: a stranger's orange on a long train was worth more than any ticket.

Harold took a long breath behind his mask. He looked at the screen, then at the oxygen reading, then at Angela. For the first time in years, he asked her what she would do.

She told him. He nodded once, slowly, and picked up the phone to call the chest team. When they arrived twelve minutes later, the bleeding was exactly where Angela had said it would be. Frank survived the night. Harold went to the relatives' room himself to tell Margaret, and afterwards, when Angela handed him a cup of tea, he thanked her without looking away.

"Ella is right," Mark said. "It's very old and very cranky. Now go and help your mum."

Ella came in with a tray of pancakes, slightly lopsided. Rachel praised them loudly, which made Ella glow. Sam tipped syrup on the floor and then tried to clean it up with the tea towel, leaving a brown smear across the tiles.

Mark came in at last, grease on his cheek, holding the lawnmower's starter cord like a trophy. The engine had finally roared to life after two hours of effort. He sat down at the table, ate a pancake in four bites, and asked whether there was any coffee left.

Rachel laughed and poured him a cup. Outside the window the garden was wet and bright, and the lawn could finally be cut. Ella declared that she would help push the mower, and Sam insisted he would ride on it. Nobody argued, and for once the morning was exactly as loud and messy as it was supposed to be.
