Nurse Imelda Okafor, who never forgot a name, began at six by greeting every bed on Ward 4 aloud. She said "Good morning, Mr. Hale" to bed nine, though he hadn't spoken in three days.

At seven Dr. Tomasz Weiss, the registrar, arrived with cold coffee and a habit of explaining everything twice. He told Mrs. Adeyemi's daughter about the broken hip, then told her again, slower, until her shoulders finally dropped.

In the sluice room, healthcare assistant Priya Nair changed linen and hummed hymns off-key. Patients began asking for her by tune.

At noon the porter, Desmond Clarke, pushed the lunch trolley in forty minutes late and told every patient the soup was excellent. It was not. Nobody minded.

At three, pharmacist Greta Lindqvist, who trusted no number she hadn't checked twice, stopped Dr. Weiss in the corridor. His heparin dose for bed fourteen was ten times too high, a misplaced decimal. He stared at the chart, thanked her instead of bristling, and rewrote it while she watched.

By evening the ward had gone quiet. Imelda made her last round, saying each name again, softly. At bed nine she said, "Goodnight, Mr. Hale," and felt his fingers close around her wrist.

She stood a moment, listening to Priya humming somewhere down the corridor and Desmond's empty trolley rattling toward the lifts. Then she pressed the bell, and Dr. Weiss came running and explained it to her twice.

text:
At 8:40 a.m., Priya Raman, the lead engineer, pushed a database migration to production and went to refill her coffee. By 8:52, Tomás, the intern, noticed the dashboard showed zero customers.

"Zero is wrong," he said, and said it louder when Priya didn't turn around.

She ran back to her desk, read the logs, and went silent. The migration had dropped the customers table. The last good backup was from Tuesday.

Across town, Dana Okafor, the founder, was pitching an investor named Mr. Halvorsen, who wanted to see the live product at 10:00. Priya called her. Dana excused herself mid-sentence, stood in a hallway that smelled of floor wax, and said, "Tell me you can fix this in an hour."

"I can restore Tuesday. Everything since is gone."

Meanwhile Walt Brennan, the office manager, discovered the building's internet had been cut for cable repairs, a notice buried in an email he'd never opened. He climbed onto a chair, held his phone toward the ceiling to find a signal, and handed Priya his hotspot like a lit torch.

Tomás, eager to help, brought her a fresh latte and tipped it across her keyboard. Priya typed the remaining commands on Walt's laptop, jaw tight, saying nothing.

At 9:58 the restore finished. At 10:00 Dana opened her laptop in the pitch room. Halvorsen watched the demo, nodded slowly, and asked why Wednesday's signups were missing.

"Because we broke something this morning," Dana said, "and I'd rather show you how we recovered than pretend we didn't."

Halvorsen wrote something down. Dana couldn't tell whether it was a check or a goodbye.

Back at the office, Walt was ordering donuts, and Tomás was apologizing to a keyboard.

text:
Saturday morning, Dana cracked six eggs into a blue bowl while the radio muttered about rain. Through the window she could see the garage door propped open, and her husband Tomas lying on his back under the lawnmower, a wrench in his fist.

"Mama, can I stir?" Pilar, who was six, dragged a chair to the counter and climbed up before anyone answered.

"Gently," Dana said, handing over the whisk. Pilar stirred like she was churning butter, and yolk splashed across the counter, the radio, and Dana's sleeve.

In the garage, nine-year-old Wes stood beside his father's boots. "What's broken?"

"The blade bolt is stripped," Tomas said from underneath. "Hand me the half-inch socket. The silver one."

Wes held up a screwdriver. Then a tape measure. Then, finally, the right socket, which he dropped on Tomas's chest.

"Thank you," Tomas wheezed.

Inside, Pilar abandoned the whisk to feed bread into the toaster, slice after slice. Dana lifted her down, rescued the toast, and flipped the first pancake, which landed perfectly.

"Breakfast!" she called through the open door.

Wes and Tomas arrived together, both with black streaks of grease across their foreheads. Wes had been helping by wiping his hands on his face.

The mower still would not start. The pancakes, stacked tall and golden, vanished in ten minutes. Tomas wiped syrup from Pilar's chin with his greasy thumb, and Dana decided the lawn could grow one more week.

Nico's forehead burned against Elena's palm at 6:40, and the thermometer beeped its verdict: 102.1.

"I have the Hartwell pitch at nine," Elena said, already pulling her laptop bag off the hook. "Eight months of work, Tomas."

Tomas stood in the kitchen doorway, buttering toast he wasn't going to eat. "And I have the budget review. The one where they decide whether my whole team exists in January."

"You said that last month about a different meeting."

"That one was real too." He set the knife down. "You stayed home for the ear infection. It's my turn."

"I stayed because you were in Denver. That wasn't a turn, that was a rescue."

From the couch, wrapped in his dinosaur blanket, Nico coughed and said, in a small scratchy voice, "I can stay by myself."

Both of them turned. He was six.

Elena exhaled. She crouched beside him and tucked the blanket under his chin. Tomas leaned on the arm of the couch.

"Your pitch can't move," Tomas said. "Mine can. Gerald owes me, and the review is a conference call anyway. I can dial in from the kitchen table."

"You'd be on mute, hiding behind a laptop, while he asks for juice."

"I'd be on mute with a kid on my lap." He smiled, a little crooked. "Go. Knock them flat."

Elena kissed Nico's hot forehead, then Tomas's cheek, and grabbed her keys.

"Soup is in the freezer," she called from the door. "The orange bowl, not the blue one."

"I know which bowl," Tomas said, and Nico giggled.

Premise: A teenager announces at dinner what they want to become, and each parent reacts differently.
text:
Lena set down her fork on Thursday night, between the last of the lentil soup and the bread, and said, "I'm going to be a taxidermist."

Her father, Marcus, laughed so hard he had to put down his spoon. Then he saw her face and stopped. "You mean that."

"I stuffed the fox that died on Henderson Road. Mr. Okafor at the natural history museum said my seams were clean."

Her mother, Priya, did not look up from her plate. She tore the bread into small, even pieces, one after another, until the heel was gone. "What does it pay?" she asked.

"Not much at first. Maybe forty thousand. Museums, hunters, a few collectors."

"And the insurance?"

"Priya," Marcus said.

"I'm asking a question. Somebody in this house should."

Marcus pushed his chair back and walked to the garage. Lena heard the door bang, then the scrape of a shelf. He came back carrying a dusty glass case: a pheasant, slightly lopsided, one eye a different shade than the other.

"My grandfather made this," he said. "I've been ashamed of it for thirty years. Hid it behind the paint cans so nobody would ask." He set it on the table between the soup bowls. "Can you fix the eye?"

Lena leaned in, studied the glass, and nodded. "And the left wing is wired wrong."

Priya finally looked up. She studied the pheasant, then her daughter's steady hands. "Forty thousand is not enough," she said. "Learn taxes. Learn how to invoice. Then do it."

"Deal," Lena said, and reached for the pliers in her pocket.

text:
Walt had forgotten how loud a house could get. By nine on Saturday morning, his granddaughter Priya, nine years old, had taught him a card game whose rules changed every time he won, and her brother Theo, six, had hidden Walt's reading glasses in the freezer for reasons he declined to explain.

"They're with the peas," Theo finally admitted, after Walt had searched the bathroom, the garage, and his own coat pockets twice.

In the kitchen, his wife Dolores stood at the stove with flour up to her elbows, attempting the pancakes she had made for their own children forty years ago. The first batch came out like gray coasters. Priya ate one anyway, with great ceremony, and announced it was "crunchy in an interesting way."

By afternoon, Walt's knees ached from crouching behind the couch as the monster in Theo's game. Dolores sat on the porch steps and braided Priya's hair, fumbling the pattern, until Priya reached back and guided her fingers over the strands.

"Like this, Grandma. Over, under, over."

"Your mother never let me do it this way," Dolores said.

"Mom does it fast," Priya said. "You do it slow. I like slow."

Sunday evening, Anna's headlights swung across the living room wall. Theo, half asleep on Walt's shoulder, mumbled, "Can we stay one more night?"

Walt looked at Dolores over the boy's head. She was holding Priya's sleeping bag, and she didn't let go of it right away.

"Ask your mom," Walt said, though his voice cracked on the last word, and neither child noticed.

Premise: During a crisis at work, one colleague stays calm and takes charge while another falls apart.
text:
At 2:40 on Friday afternoon, the payroll server at Harlow Freight went dark, eleven minutes before the bank's transfer deadline for four hundred drivers.

Priya Nair did not raise her voice. She set down her coffee, pulled her laptop closer, and said, "Okay. Everyone stop typing for a second."

Desmond Okafor, the finance analyst, was already standing, both hands pressed against his scalp. "We're done. They won't get paid. They'll walk out Monday, and it's on me, I approved the migration."

"Desmond, sit down." Priya's tone was mild, almost kind. "Tell me the last thing you saw before it crashed."

He slid down the wall to the floor. His breath came in hitches. "The batch file. It said something about a lock."

"Good. That's useful." She turned to the new hire. "Marguerite, call the bank's emergency line and ask for a two-hour extension. Read them our account number off the card in my top drawer. Don't apologize, just ask."

Marguerite Duval nodded and ran.

Priya opened a terminal, found the stuck process Desmond had described, and killed it. She restarted the service while Desmond muttered about updating his résumé.

"Desmond," she said without looking up. "I need the timesheets exported by hand, in case the restart fails. You know that spreadsheet better than anyone. Can you do that?"

He wiped his face on his sleeve. Then he got up, slowly, and sat beside her.

At 2:48, Marguerite returned, breathless. "Two hours. They said yes."

The files went through at 3:22. Priya finally drank her coffee. It was cold. She drank it anyway, and Desmond, still pale, laughed for the first time all day.

Premise: Two siblings: one is brave and reckless, the other is careful and sensitive. They get lost in the woods.
text:
Dara spotted the shortcut at four o'clock, a deer trail bending away from the path, and she was through the ferns before her brother finished saying her name.

"Dara, the markers," Ilan called. He stood at the edge of the path, gripping his backpack straps, counting the blue ribbons tied to the birches. Seven. The eighth was missing.

"Come on, Ilan. It's faster."

It was not faster. By five o'clock the deer trail had split into three, then into nothing, and the light under the spruce trees had turned the color of weak tea. Dara climbed a boulder and shouted hello into the woods, loud enough to scatter the crows. Nothing answered.

"Stop yelling," Ilan whispered. His eyes were wet, and he turned his face away so she wouldn't see. "You'll make it worse."

"Worse than lost?"

He didn't reply. Instead he crouched and studied the moss on the nearest trunk, then the slope of the ground, then the faint hush underneath the forest noise. "Water," he said. "Hear it? The creek ran beside the parking lot. If we follow it downhill, it comes out where Dad parked."

Dara leaped off the boulder, ready to charge toward the sound. Ilan caught her sleeve.

"Slowly. Test every rock before you step."

She rolled her eyes but obeyed. Ilan went first, tapping logs with a stick, and Dara followed with one hand on his shoulder, searching the shadows for bears she secretly hoped to see.

At dusk they heard a car horn. Their father, Anselm, stood beside the truck, swinging his flashlight. Dara sprinted ahead, whooping. Ilan walked, and he was the first one hugged.

Premise: Two people negotiate the price of a used car. One is tough, the other gives in.
text:
Gerald Pruitt had washed his 2012 Corolla twice that morning, and it still smelled faintly of the dog he no longer owned. He stood in his Dayton driveway, keys in his fist, while Imani Okafor circled the car, crouching at each wheel.

"Your ad says forty-two hundred," she said.

"It does. And a hundred and twelve thousand miles is nothing for a Toyota."

Imani ran a thumbnail along a rust bubble above the rear wheel arch. "That's rust. The tires are two winters from bald. The check-engine light came on when I turned the key, and you didn't mention it." She straightened. "Three thousand."

Gerald laughed, but it came out thin. "The light is just a sensor. My brother-in-law looked at it."

"Then your brother-in-law can have it for three thousand." She pulled out her phone and scrolled through other listings without looking up. She had bought four cars in her life and had never paid sticker on any of them.

Gerald glanced at the house, where his wife, Lorraine, watched from the kitchen window with her arms folded. The transmission on his own truck was due at the shop Friday. He needed the money, but more than the money, he needed this to be over.

"Thirty-five hundred," he said.

"Thirty-two."

"Thirty-three, and I'll throw in the floor mats."

Imani finally looked up. "Thirty-two fifty, with the mats."

Gerald's shoulders dropped. "Fine. Fine."

He handed her the keys. She counted the cash onto the hood, bill by bill, while he stared at the dent in his garage door that he had never fixed.

They reached the top at noon. Priya unwrapped the sandwiches she had made the night before, handed one to each, and sat down last.

"Good call, boss," Marcus said.

Priya laughed and threw her crust at him.

On Saturday Dolores knocked on number 14 with a lemon cake. Emi accepted it with both hands and bowed slightly, and Dolores, surprised at herself, bowed back.

By Sunday evening Yuki had taped a drawing inside the Whitcombs' mailbox: the maple tree, a mower, and three small figures on a lawn, one of them with his arms uncrossed.

Premise: A shopkeeper in a small border town grows suspicious of a customer who speaks with an accent.
text:
Dragomir Vesely kept the only hardware shop in Kolárovo, a town so close to the river border that the church bells rang twice, once from each side.

On Tuesday a woman came in and asked for forty meters of copper wire, a roll of insulating tape, and "the small pliers, for the delicate work." Her accent bent every vowel. She paid in coins from both currencies, counting slowly.

Dragomir watched her through the window as she walked off toward the river road. Copper wire. Pliers. He had read the notices pinned beside the post office. At supper he told his wife Ilona the stranger had been odd, and Ilona said, "Everyone is odd who isn't us."

On Thursday the woman returned and bought a battery and a screwdriver. Dragomir reached for the phone beside the till, stopped, then followed her instead, keeping thirty paces back, feeling foolish and righteous in equal measure.

She did not go to the river. She went to the schoolhouse, where Mrs. Halasová, the music teacher, stood beside a dead electric organ. The woman climbed onto a stool, opened the back panel, and began splicing wire with the delicate pliers.

"Mirela repairs organs," Mrs. Halasová called, spotting him in the doorway. "She drives in from the other side every month. Nobody here knows how."

Mirela glanced down at him. "You sold me good wire," she said.

Dragomir took off his cap. On Saturday, when the organ played its first hymn, he stood at the back and did not sing. Afterward he pressed a fresh roll of tape into Mirela's hand and refused her coins.

Premise: Three travellers from three different countries share a train compartment overnight. Say where each one is from.
text:
The night train from Vienna to Venice left at nine, and by ten the compartment held three strangers.

Ayaka Mori, a bookbinder from Kyoto, Japan, had claimed the window seat and was stitching a pamphlet with waxed thread. Across from her, Tomás Herrera, a cellist from Valparaíso, Chile, wedged his instrument case between his knees like a sleeping child. The third, Birgit Halvorsen, a retired ferry captain from Tromsø, Norway, unwrapped a wedge of brown cheese and offered it around without a word.

Tomás took a slice. "Is it always this salty?"

"It's goat," Birgit said. "Salt is the point."

Ayaka laughed, bit off her thread, and held the needle to the lamp. Near Villach the train braked hard for a signal, and the compartment lurched. Birgit caught the cheese with one hand and Tomás's case with the other.

"Thirty years on water," she said. "My hands know a swell."

"He is my uncle."

The meter ticked past forty dollars. Rain began, smearing the red taillights along the expressway into long ribbons. Rosario told him which train to take, the M, and which stop to get off at, and that the bakery door stuck in winter, so you had to lift as you pushed. She made him say it back twice.

At two in the morning she pulled up outside a narrow brick building with a lit window above the awning. Tomasz counted out his bills, hesitated, and added another twenty.

"Keep it," Rosario said, passing it back through the partition. "Bring me a loaf of rye when you're running the place."

"I will not be running the place."

"Sure you will," she said, and she waited at the curb until the upstairs light came on and a man's silhouette lifted one hand to the glass.

"I'll open the door," Daniel said. "I'm not promising anyone walks in."

Priya walked him through the floor. Marcus kept his eyes on the carpet, counting the treadmills, the mirrors, the men who seemed to be made of rope. By the dumbbells, a gray-haired man named Walt was resting between sets, a towel around his neck.

"Don't pick the machine in the corner," Walt said, without being asked. "That's where I hid for a year."

Marcus blinked. "What changed?"

"My doctor said a number out loud. And my granddaughter asked why I couldn't chase her." Walt shrugged. "So I came out of the corner."

Priya set Marcus up on a treadmill in the middle of the room. He pressed the button, and the belt began to move at 1.5 miles per hour, slower than a stroll.

Five minutes later his shirt stuck to his back, his calves burned, and his heart thudded like someone knocking on a door.

"Nice work," Walt called over, lifting a dumbbell. "Same time tomorrow?"

Marcus wiped his face. "Same time tomorrow."

"I never said he was found near the stairs." She held up the brass key. "Elias took this from your pocket, didn't he? It opens the vault where you hid the forged star charts."

Victor lunged for the door, but Marguerite caught his wrist and snapped the handcuffs shut. Outside, the rain stopped, and the first stars appeared through the open dome.

In Thistlewick, where the road gives up and becomes a footpath, six people keep everything running.

Odile Marsh, the baker, lights her oven at three every morning, and by dawn the whole village smells of rye and cardamom. Nobody argues before they've eaten her bread.

Bram Holloway, the blacksmith, mends whatever breaks: ploughshares, hinges, and once a child's cracked skate blade, which he fixed for free and pretended he hadn't.

Dr. Wen Adeyemi rides a bicycle with a leather bag strapped to the handlebars. She sets bones, delivers babies, and tells the old men, firmly, to stop climbing ladders.

Ines Quartermain teaches twenty-two children in the single schoolroom. She teaches sums, but mostly she teaches them to ask why, which their parents sometimes regret.

Hester Vance runs the post office from her front parlour. She reads every postcard before delivering it, and in forty years she has never repeated a word, which is why people trust her with their worst news.

Last is Pell Sorensen, the mayor, who has no real authority except the key to the bell tower. When the river rises or a stranger arrives or a wedding begins, Pell rings, and everyone comes.

Last winter the river did rise. Pell rang the bell, Bram hauled sandbags, Odile carried baskets of bread, Wen carried bandages, Ines marched the children up the hill in a line, and Hester produced her list of who lived in which house. By morning, nobody was missing.

At seven sharp a man in a green scarf came in, scanning the room. Tomas Beaumont, principal dancer with the city ballet, according to the friend who had set this up. He crossed the floor so smoothly that the waiters stepped aside without noticing they had done it.

"You must be Priya," he said, and sat. "Sorry, I'm still warm. Late rehearsal."

"You're not warm," Priya said. "Your hands are shaking."

Tomas looked down. "Tendons. They do that after six hours of jumps."

"What's the actual mechanism?" She pulled out a pen and reached for a napkin, then stopped. "Sorry. I do this."

"Do it," he said, and he meant it. He drew a leg on the napkin, and she corrected his Achilles. Then he leaned over and tapped the base of her spine with one finger. "Ribs down. You're holding your breath."

She exhaled, and discovered he was right.

By the time the pasta came, he was explaining counts in eights while she tapped them out on the tablecloth with her pen, and she was explaining why her protein crystals refused to grow, and neither of them was eating.

Marguerite came in with her coffee and stopped in the doorway.

"Well," she said quietly. "There it is."

Daniel looked up from his homework. "That's the four minutes."

At 3:10 a.m., Nurse Delia Marsh found Dr. Ravi Koenig in the surgical lounge, eating crackers out of a vending-machine sleeve.

"Mr. Ostrowski in bed nine," she said. "His belly's changed."

Ravi didn't look up. "He's two days out from a bowel resection. Bellies change."

"Not like this. It was soft at midnight. Now it's tight as a drum, and he guards when I press. Heart rate went from eighty-eight to one-twelve."

"Fever?"

"Thirty-eight point one."

Ravi brushed salt from his scrubs. "That's pain and dehydration. Bolus him a liter, bump his morphine, and I'll see him at rounds."

Delia stayed in the doorway. She had worked the surgical floor for nineteen years; Ravi had been an attending for four. She had watched him do flawless work under the lights, and she had also watched him go grey when a patient crashed at dawn on a night he'd chosen to sleep.

"Leonard Ostrowski asked me to call his daughter, Agnes," she said. "He told me something feels wrong. He's not a complainer, Doctor. He apologized for using the call bell."

"Feelings aren't vital signs."

"Then come look at his vital signs."

Ravi sighed and stood. In bed nine, Leonard lay curled on his side, sweat beading at his hairline. Ravi laid two fingers below the incision, and Leonard cried out before he had pressed at all.

Ravi straightened slowly. He looked at the monitor, then at Delia.

"So we both want to be invisible," Hannah said.

In 14C, Gerald Pike did not stay seated. He unbuckled, stood, and grabbed the overhead bin as the floor fell again. His coffee sloshed across the aisle onto Priya Shah, a sleeping teenager in 14D.

"We're going down!" Gerald shouted. "The engine stopped. I felt it."

Teo Marchetti, the flight attendant, was strapped into his jump seat by the galley. He waited for the next bump to pass, then unclipped and worked his way up the aisle, one hand on every seatback.

"Gerald, right?" Teo had read the name off the manifest. "The engines are fine. Listen." He tilted his head. Under the rattling bins, the steady roar held.

Gerald's knuckles stayed white on the latch. "How would you know?"

Teo lifted the interphone at row twelve and called the cockpit. "Captain, can you talk to 14C?"

Ruth keyed the PA. "Gerald, this is Ruth Okafor. I'm flying this airplane. Both engines are running normally. We're climbing to smoother air. Ten more minutes."

Gerald looked at Teo. Teo guided him back down, fastened Gerald's belt for him, then dropped into the empty seat behind and rested a hand on his shoulder.

"Breathe with me," Teo said. "In for four. Out for four."

They were on their ninth breath when the shaking stopped. Gerald unclenched his fingers and passed Priya a stack of napkins.

"Sorry," he said.

"I'm Grace," she said. "He told me everything last night. He told me about you."

Marta climbed up and scooped out the wet leaves with her bare hands. From the top rung she could see the whole street: Len on his phone, Pauline's curtain twitching, Leela hurrying the children indoors.

"You going to leave us, then?" Stanley called up.

Marta dropped a fistful of leaves into his bucket. "Haven't decided," she said. "Hold the ladder steady."

He did.

Rain was still dripping from the awning when Detective Ines Okafor ducked under the police tape at Halloran's Clocks. She was a short, broad woman of fifty, with cropped grey hair, a chipped front tooth, and a raincoat two sizes too big that had belonged to her late husband.

The victim, Tobias Halloran, lay behind the counter. He had been thin as a coat hanger, seventy or so, with a white moustache waxed to two points and ink-stained fingers. A brass mantel clock had crushed the side of his skull. His jeweler's loupe still hung from a cord around his neck.

Okafor knelt and studied his hands. Under his right thumbnail was a thread of mustard-yellow wool.

Every clock in the shop ticked along correctly, except one, a cheap carriage clock on the shelf, stopped at 9:40. Okafor opened its back and found a folded pawn ticket made out to Lucian Vane.

The engine of the Marigold died during breakfast. The hum everyone had stopped hearing simply ended, and Oskar Lindqvist, the cook, watched the porridge in his pot go still.

Captain Amara Osei reached the bridge in forty seconds. Navigator Tomas Reyes already had the numbers up. "We're coasting at the same speed, but we're off the transfer line," he said. "In nine days we miss Ceres by two million kilometers, and then there's nothing."

Down in the engine bay, Chief Engineer Yuki Tanabe pulled the injector housing and swore at it. A coolant seal had cracked and the fuel line behind it had fused solid. She could machine a new line, she told the captain over the intercom, but she needed a heat-proof seal, and the stores had none.

Then Ilse Brandt, the security chief, carried Yuki up from the bay with her left hand wrapped in a scorched rag. Dr. Farid Nazari cleaned the burn in the infirmary and dressed it with silicone gel sheeting. Yuki stared at the sheet on her palm.

"How hot can that take?"

"This? Not very," Farid said. "Why?"

Oskar, bringing porridge, overheard. He went back to the galley and returned with his oven door gasket, a thick ring of ceramic-weave rated for years of roasting.

Yuki worked one-handed for two days, with Ilse holding the clamps and swearing on her behalf. Tomas recalculated the burn four times, each window narrower than the last.

On the third morning, Amara gave the order. The hum returned, thin and uneven, and held.

Oskar served cold sandwiches for the rest of the voyage. Nobody complained.

"Before sunrise," she said. "At the root."

He took it. The following week, he cut a gate in the wire.

On the fourth floor, someone had moved her desk plant to the window. It had grown two new leaves. She stood looking at it with her coat still on until Tomasz Bell wheeled his chair across the aisle.

"I watered it," he said. "Badly, at first. I looked it up in March."

"Thanks, Tomasz."

He nodded, opened his mouth, closed it. Renata had rehearsed this with Dr. Haddad: people will not know what to say, and that will not be your job to fix. So she sat down and let the silence belong to both of them.

At ten, Priya Nair from accounts stopped by with a voice pitched for hospital rooms. "You look so well," she said, and squeezed Renata's shoulder. Renata thanked her, and noticed she was counting her breaths, and noticed that the counting worked.

The inbox held four thousand messages. Her manager, Joan Whitlock, had sent one that morning: "Delete all of it. Half days until June, like we agreed. The Harmon file is yours when you want it, not before."

At noon, Renata's hands had begun to shake slightly, so she walked to the kitchen and ran them under the cold tap. Tomasz came in behind her and took two mugs from the cupboard without asking.

"The machine's still broken," he said. "You have to hit it on the left."

"You can ask," Tomasz said. "Everybody gets around to it by October."

Dele sat up, hot in the face. "I wasn't... okay. What's the half hour for?"

"Thyroid. They took mine out when I was sixteen. The pill is my whole thyroid now, and it sulks if it meets coffee." He shrugged. "So, thirty minutes of staring at the car park. Forever. That's the tragic part."

Dele laughed too loudly, from a relief he hadn't earned.

The next morning, when the timer rang at seven-forty, Dele was standing in the doorway with two coffees from the machine downstairs. Tomasz took his without comment, and hummed.

"To Mr. Desmond Pike, Pike and Sons Haulage," he said. "Sir. Your conduct regarding the October shipment has been a disgrace."

Maureen Doyle's pencil moved across the steno pad. She had taken his dictation for thirty-one years, through two recessions and his first wife.

"Strike disgrace. Make it a betrayal."

She struck it.

"I gave you your first contract when no one in this county would trust you with a wheelbarrow. I stood up at your wedding."

Rain ticked against the glass. Below, a forklift carried the last pallet into the empty half of the warehouse. Harold watched it go.

"I expect full payment by Friday, or you will hear from my attorneys." He paused. "Read that back."

Maureen read it back in her flat, unhurried voice. Hearing it, Harold rubbed the bald spot on his crown.

"Is it too hard?"

"You don't have attorneys," Maureen said. "You let Feldman go in March."

Harold turned from the window. He looked at the pad, then at her cardigan, darned at one elbow in the wrong shade of blue.

"Strike the attorneys."

She struck them.

"Write this. Desmond. Your mother would be ashamed of us both. Come by on Sunday and bring the invoice, and we'll sort it over a drink."

Maureen wrote it, tore the sheet free, and rolled it into the typewriter.

"Sign it Harold?" she asked.

He sat down heavily. "Sign it Harry. He's the only one left who calls me that."

Premise: A programmer fixes a bug at three in the morning.
text:
The radiator in Tomasz Wrona's flat knocked twice, the way it did every night at three, and he looked up from the log file he had been reading for two hours.

The bakery's ordering system kept charging customers twice, but only on the last Sunday of October. His sister, Hania, owned the bakery. She had called him at dinner, trying not to cry, with forty-one refunds written on the back of a flour invoice.

He scrolled again. Order placed 02:14. Payment retried 02:14. He pulled a cold pierogi off the plate, chewed, and stopped chewing.

The clocks. The clocks had gone back that morning, so 02:14 had happened twice. The retry job compared local timestamps, saw an order an hour younger than it should be, decided the payment had never gone through, and charged the card again. Tomasz had written that job himself, four years ago, as a favour, on Hania's kitchen table.

He changed three lines so the job compared UTC. He wrote a test that set the clock to the bad hour, watched it fail, then watched it pass. The cat, Bajka, walked across the keyboard and added a row of semicolons, which he deleted without looking at her.

He pushed the fix at 3:26.

Then he opened a message to Hania and typed a long explanation about daylight saving time. He read it over, deleted all of it, and wrote instead: "Fixed. My fault. I'll do the refunds tomorrow. Save me a rye."

Her reply came at 4:50, when she lit the ovens.

"Two ryes."

Premise: A cleaner finds something unexpected in an office at night.
text:
Marisol Vega reached the fourteenth floor at a quarter past one, pushing her cart past the dark glass of Hartwell Insurance. She always saved Mr. Okafor's corner office for last because it needed the least. He ate no lunch at his desk and left no rings on the wood.

Tonight a lamp was on. Under it, on the blotter, sat a saucer of milk.

Marisol frowned and lifted the saucer. The milk was fresh. Something scraped behind the filing cabinet, and she set down her spray bottle and crouched with her flashlight.

Two green eyes looked back. A kitten, grey and barely bigger than her fist, had wedged itself against the wall on a folded cardigan. Beside it lay a tin of tuna and a sheet of paper in Mr. Okafor's tidy hand: *Feed at 6, 12, 6. Do not tell Dunleavy.*

Dunleavy was the building manager. He had once fined a tenant over a goldfish.

Marisol eased the kitten out. It bit her thumb with no conviction at all, then fell asleep against her wrist.

She thought about the paper, and about Mr. Okafor, who had nodded at her for six years without once saying a word. She had assumed he was cold. Now she noticed a scratch across the leather of his chair and small tooth marks on his expensive pen.

She changed the milk, because it had been sitting since six. She folded the cardigan fresh. Then she took a pencil and wrote beneath his instructions: *Midnight feed is covered. Her name is Pepa. — M.V., cleaning.*

In the morning, a second tin of tuna waited on her cart, with a thank-you note.

Premise: A lighthouse keeper during the worst storm in a decade.
text:
By nine o'clock the sea was coming over the gallery rail, ninety feet up, and Maren Oakes had stopped writing in the log because the ink kept jumping.

She climbed the last ladder with a can of paraffin in one hand. The mantle had blown out twice since dusk. Each time she relit it, the lens floated round on its mercury bath as calmly as a plate on a still pond, while the whole tower shivered beneath it like a struck bell.

The radio crackled. "Skerry Light, this is Tomas at the harbour. You still standing?"

"Standing," Maren said. "What's out?"

"The Halloran boat. Dessa and her boy. They left the banks at noon."

Maren looked west and saw nothing but black water heaving against black sky. Then a window on the landing below burst inward, and the wind came up the stairwell and snuffed the flame a third time.

The matches were soaked. She pulled the spare box from inside her shirt, where she had carried it since supper, struck one, and cupped it with her whole body. It caught. She stayed crouched there, her burned thumb in her mouth, and did not leave the lamp again.

She trimmed it every quarter hour until the window went grey. At six she saw a small green hull wallowing past the reef, low in the water, with one figure bailing and another at the tiller.

She picked up the radio. "Tomas. Tell them the Hallorans are coming in."

Then she opened the log, steadied her hand, and wrote: Wind severe. Light maintained.

Premise: A robot learns to paint.
text:
Tomasz Wrona bought the robot at a factory auction, because it was cheap and could lift forty kilos. He named it Bolt and set it to hauling canvas stretchers around his studio above the fish market.

For three years Bolt carried things and watched. Then one wet February morning, Tomasz came upstairs and found the robot holding a size-six filbert in its welding claw, standing before a primed board.

On the board was a grey rectangle, perfectly even, edge to edge.

"What's that?" Tomasz asked.

"The window," Bolt said. "I have matched its value to within two percent."

Tomasz laughed until he coughed. Then he took the brush, loaded it badly, and dragged a crooked streak of ochre across the grey.

"You've ruined it," Bolt said.

"Now look at the window."

Bolt turned its lenses. Rain ran down the glass. A gull hung over the market, and below it Hanna Novak was hosing scales off her stall, her yellow oilskin flaring each time she bent.

For eleven weeks Bolt painted Hanna's oilskin. Tomasz scraped each attempt off with a palette knife and said, "Too correct." Bolt logged the phrase and could not define it.

In May, Tomasz's hands began to shake, and he could no longer hold a line. Bolt ground his colours and said nothing about it.

One evening, Bolt's left servo seized mid-stroke. The claw jerked, and yellow skidded wide across the board. Bolt reached for the knife, then stopped.

Tomasz leaned in, breathing hard, and studied the skid for a long time.

"There she is," he said. "That's Hanna, bending."

Bolt put down the knife and did not repair the servo.

Premise: Two friends open a bakery and the first week goes badly.
text:
On Monday the oven ran forty degrees hot, and nobody knew it until Marit Solberg pulled out sixty croissants the color of old saddles. Dessa Okafor, who had remortgaged a two-bedroom flat for this, ate one standing up and said it tasted like a campfire with ambitions.

They sold eleven coffees and gave away the croissants to a roofing crew, who were polite about it.

On Tuesday Marit bought an oven thermometer. On Wednesday the water main on Pell Street burst, and the council closed the pavement outside their door with orange barriers, so that customers would have had to climb to reach them. Two did. One wanted directions.

Thursday, Dessa misread her own handwriting and put two kilos of salt in the brioche instead of two hundred grams. Marit tasted the dough, looked at her, and said nothing for a full minute. Then she tipped it into the bin and started washing the mixer, and Dessa sat down on a flour sack and cried, loudly, the way she did at weddings.

"We can still get out," Dessa said. "Sell the mixer. Tell my mother I was robbed."

Marit dried her hands. "Your mother would ask for the police report."

On Saturday they took in ninety-four pounds and spent three hundred. At closing, a small boy named Teo came in with his grandfather and pointed at the last tray, the ugly rye rolls Marit had nearly thrown out. The grandfather bought all six. He came back ten minutes later, alone, a little out of breath.

"Monday," he said. "What time do you open?"

Dessa turned the sign over and told him seven.

Premise: A lost dog finds its way home across a city.
text:
The firecracker went off behind the fish market, and Biscuit slipped her collar and ran until her paws bled. When she stopped, nothing smelled of anything she knew.

She was a brindle mutt with one folded ear, and for two days she walked the wrong way along the ring road, drinking from gutters. On the third morning the wind turned and carried a thin thread of burnt sugar. That was the Marek bakery, four streets from home. Biscuit put her nose into it and followed.

The river stopped her. She paced the embankment until Tomasz, a tram driver eating his lunch on the steps, tossed her a crust and watched her limp onto the footbridge behind a line of schoolchildren. A girl named Odile held out a hand. Biscuit sniffed it, licked the salt off, and kept walking.

Past the bridge came the rail yards, where a yellow dog bit her shoulder over a chicken bone. Biscuit let him have it. She crawled under the fence and slept beneath a parked lorry until the cold woke her and the sugar smell rose again, stronger now, because Mrs. Marek lit her ovens at four.

Grey light was coming when she turned onto Linden Street. Every lamppost carried a paper with her face on it, and the ink had run in the rain.

Jonah, nine years old, sat on the front step in his coat, where he had sat every morning that week. He looked up from his cereal bowl. The spoon hit the pavement.

Biscuit did not run. She walked the last ten metres, leaned her whole weight against his knees, and slept.
